#779. Pochettino’s fiery start, plus England v All Blacks and ATP Finals finale – follow with us

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The international break is over as domestic football boogies back. Primed to feel the force is Dominic Booth at the helm of our essential gateway to the weekend’s action. Saturday offers a magnificent seven Premier League matches, bookended by Manchester City v Fulham and Newcastle v Arsenal. There is also a full programme of Championship, League One, and League Two fixtures, plus Celtic and Rangers taking to the Glasgow greensward in Scotland. In the WSL, Liverpool host Chelsea before rich kids London City prepare to receive Crystal Palace. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday.live@theguardian.com.

To the background buzz of Australian cricket ripping itself apart over sandpapergate, England kick off their T20 series at the same venue they became world champions four years ago. The Melbourne Cricket Ground has not always been a happy hunting ground for touring England sides but Harry Brook’s last two visits as captain have been triumphant. A two-day win at the 90,000-capacity venue in last year’s Boxing Day Test was not only the high point of a traumatic Ashes campaign; it was their first red-ball victory on Australian soil since 2011. MCG also hosted England’s T20 World Cup triumph in 2022, where Brook was part of the side that defeated Pakistan to lift the trophy behind enemy lines. Rob Smyth has over-by-over coverage with Ali Martin reporting from Melbourne.

The lunchtime kick-off is a vital one for the hosts. City have wobbled of late, three straight Premier League defeats leave the beleaguered club in third with 21 points from the first 10 games of Enzo Maresca’s tenure. In stark contrast, the Cottagers are unbeaten in their last four games, after four defeats and two draws in their first six. Wins over Hull and Coventry came before draws with Aston Villa and Newcastle. Barry Glendenning helms the blog as Will Unwin reports from the Etihad Stadium.

England are have been transformed since stumbling through the Six Nations and then falling to South Africa at Ellis Park, winning four consecutive Tests, amassing 36 tries and addressing their disciplinary lapses. Aided by thumping victories over Fiji and Japan, they have rebuilt impressively to secure a shot at reaching the Nations Championship final, but New Zealand provide the true measure of their progress. Only South Africa are higher in the rankings and a year out from the 2027 World Cup final, it is the opportunity for Steve Borthwick’s men to make a statement. Lee Calvert blogs the action and the trio of Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher making up our Twickenham reporting team.

Katy Murrells is at the controls of our tennis liveblog as the semi-finals pan out in Turin. The first session starts at 2.30pm, with the evening match due to start at about 8.30pm.

Emillia Hawkins keeps the updates flowing on the five afternoon kick-offs: Aston Villa v Sunderland, Bournemouth v Nottingham Forest, Chelsea v Leeds, Coventry v Crystal Palace, and Tottenham v Ipswich – the pick of the bunch. Roberto De Zerbi seemed to be making an impact at Spurs before a defeat by Leeds tripped up his side. Their record is grim against the Tractor Boys: four defeats in their last five Premier league games.

Lee Calvert is back on deck as Ireland risk a Springbok backlash from a side bruised by defeat by France and furious at their coach, Rassie Erasmus, for getting banned after his incendiary “match-fixing” comments. There is more at stake in this November’s meeting between the sides than last year’s chaotic Test. The Irish were down to 12 men at one stage and the Springboks won 24-13 for their first win in Dublin since 2012. Both countries are still in the running to top their respective pools and play in the final on Finals weekend at Twickenham. Brendan Fanning reports.

City’s slump has allowed the defending champions, Arsenal, to seize early control and they will hope to continue their relentless start to the season. They head to Newcastle where a toxic reception awaits Bruno Guimarães as he returns to Tyneside in Arsenal colours for the first time since his summer move. The Gunners are five points clear of second-placed Brighton at the top after winning nine of their first 10 games. Matthias Jaissle’s inconsistent hosts have managed just one win in their past five league matches, losing to Everton and Aston Villa along the way. Join Rob Smyth for MBM commentary, with Louis Taylor reporting.

Kimi Antonelli may have already won the drivers’ crown, but second place in the standings is still up for grabs and Max Verstappen can tighten his grip in Sin City. The Red Bull driver is 17 points clear of Mercedes’ George Russell, who moved back up to third place, one point ahead of Lewis Hamilton after his fourth place at Interlagos. Krishani Dhanji be live blogging the race in the small hours, with Giles Richards reporting from Las Vegas.

Dominic Booth and Emillia Hawkins clock on with all the latest news and reader views for a Sunday featuring the Premier League fixture of the weekend. Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of Manchester United at Anfield just days after wrapping up his reign as USA men’s coach. Victory would give him instant momentum as he fights to lift the club up the table. Earlier, hard-charging Brighton will fancy their chances against Hull, who have not won a Premier League match since August. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday.live@theguardian.com.

Emillia Hawkins and John Brewin keep track of Sunday’s WSL fixtures from midday as Birmingham face Manchester United and Charlton host Aston Villa. Then it is Everton v Brighton at 2pm followed by a London derby as Rita Guarino’s in-form West Ham visit Arsenal, with the Irons having notched four wins in their past five matches in all competitions. The Gunners are toiling, and they sit sixth in the standings going into the weekend, with just three wins from their opening 10 matches.

Second-placed Brighton have become the most unlikely title contenders with their free-scoring football and have every chance of continuing to defy the sceptics as they take on Hull. The Seagulls are the league’s top scorers with 26 goals, 11 more than Arsenal, and have the second-tightest defence, with just seven goals conceded.Join Dominic Booth for minute-by-minute coverage, with Aaron Bower reporting from MKM Stadium.

Rob Smyth buckles up for the big one at Anfield with all eyes on the latest United manager, Mauricio Pochettino. United’s tally of eight points and one win after 10 games is their lowest at this stage of a league season for 40 years. The former Southampton, Spurs and Chelsea manager says he needs time to turn the dysfunctional club’s fortunes around but he will be aware of the need to show progress quickly, with Liverpool in no mood to offer their most bitter rivals any favours. Looking for omens? The Argentinian’s first game for Chelsea was against Liverpool, which ended in a 1-1 draw at Stamford Bridge. Andy Hunter and Jamie Jackson make up our reporting team on Merseyside.

Daniel Harris offers live coverage of the final from Turin as the season-ending indoor hard-court tournament featuring the top eight singles players and top eight doubles teams draws to a thrilling close.

Graham Searles returns with his essential NFL liveblog covering the seven 6pm clashes. The division-leading Buffalo Bills (8-1), who boast the top scoring offence and second-best rush attack in the NFL, meet the Miami Dolphins (1-8) in the big AFC East clash. The other early Sunday games are Bears v Saints, Lions v Buccaneers, Panthers v Ravens, Cowboys v Titans, Chiefs v Cardinals, and Eagles v Steelers.

#778. What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?

The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.

Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

#776. Arsenal’s Lisa Baum: ‘I believe in us. I think it’s all about the small margins’

Germany forward on her new life in London and drawing strength from the memory of her late brother, Dennis

Lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

“It was unbelievable,” says Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”

That win kickstarted Arsenal’s season but it quickly stalled. In the league, the team went five games without a win. After a 2-0 defeat by OL Lyonnes in the Champions League on Thursday night, Arsenal have five wins from their opening 15 games. It is far from the season they, or many others, envisaged.

Sunday’s final home game of the year, against West Ham, offers an opportunity to take some positivity into the international break, after which Arsenal face three away fixtures before the winter pause.

“I believe in us,” says Baum. “I think it’s all about the small margins. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s in the final decision-making, sometimes it’s how close we are to a goal that doesn’t go in. But we work really hard in every training session and on trying to keep ourselves up mentally and physically. We’re trying to push through the barrier that we maybe have right now, but we get a lot of trust from the staff and coaches. Everybody really believes in each other and I think it’s not going to take long before we’re through this part of the journey.”

Overall, Arsenal have not been playing particularly badly. They have been creating chances and dominating games but struggling to translate that into goals and points. In October, Baum earned a first senior Germany call-up and made her debut off the bench at half-time against Australia, having previously featured for teams from the under-16s to under-23s.

The Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, says Pro Ref has accepted it made an error in disallowing a goal his side thought they had scored during this month's 2-1 defeat by Arsenal at Anfield.

The Women’s Super League game was level at 1-1 when Jenna Clark tucked the ball into the net after ­Arsenal had failed to clear a corner, but the assistant referee disallowed the goal for offside against Vivien ­Endemann. Replays showed the delivery had been ­inadvertently played off an Arsenal foot rather than being a deliberate forward pass from the home side. There is no VAR in the WSL.

Taylor, whose side host Chelsea in the WSL on Saturday, said on Friday: “We have had an acceptance of a mistake from the corner that we scored from, where we should be 2-1 up at half-time. [There was] no apology, but we accept that there was an error made on their part and that game can look different.” Tom Garry

Baum moved to Germany when she was four. Born to a Tanzanian mother and German father, she spent her first years in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. They swapped a city with a population of about four million for Ahrensbök, a municipality with a population of just over 8,000 near the Baltic coast. “I think my mum had the hardest time out of us in the family, with the move to Germany,” she says. Baum says she and her brother, Dennis, “learned to adapt easily”.

Baum doesn’t remember her years on the east coast of Africa but when she went back three or four years ago, some sort of memory was triggered. “It was a feeling, or feelings,” she says. “It was so good to grow up there. It was warm, it was the beautiful beaches, it was having all your family around. I was in kindergarten or I was in the water a lot – I love to swim.”

She started playing football after the move to northern Germany, desperate to copy Dennis. “My father played football when he was younger – he was a goalkeeper – but he stopped when he didn’t really enjoy it any more. My mum wasn’t a big fan of me playing; she dressed me like a girly girl, with princess dresses and that kind of stuff, but I was never really like that at that age. I always wanted to follow my older brother – I wanted to wear his clothes. He started playing football before me and I wanted to be like him.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Baum would play on the side of the pitch at her brother’s club until a parent said she should be playing too. After playing with various local teams she joined Hamburg’s academy. She worked her way into the first team and they won promotion to the second tier in her first season. In the 2024-25 season they reached the DFB-Pokal semi-finals and the top flight. Baum moved to RB Leipzig and scored five goals in 27 games before Arsenal swooped.

“Everything was just so quick,” she says of the move to London. Training required getting used to: “Everything was so sharp, everything was technically excellent, like 10 out of 10. I was quite nervous and had some clumsy actions.”

The transfer also involved swapping an average attendance last season of 1,651 for one of 33,808. “It’s unbelievable,” says Baum of playing at the Emirates Stadium. “I had only played in a big stadium once before. You can’t even believe how much the fans give you when you step on the pitch. There’s so much support, that of course we need in this current time. I think Arsenal is a club that holds on to us, on to the team, and gives us a lot of strength.”

Look closely at Baum’s left wrist when she plays and you will usually see a strip of white tape around it. Sometimes it has something written on it. She’s done it “since that day” – the day in 2022 when Dennis died in a car accident, aged 17.

The brother that inspired her on to a pitch is with her on it at the highest level. “The next time I was on the football pitch, I just felt I wanted to do that,” she says. “I feel like it’s given me a different kind of strength and confidence. Sometimes I don’t write anything, but it’s about just having the physical feeling that he is with me.”

#775. Kristen Doute's Fiancé Luke Broderick Leaves The Valley After Season 3

Kristen Doute's fiancé Luke Broderick is raising a glass to his appearance on The Valley after three seasons. As Doute put it, "That was the decision he made."

Luke Broderick is pumping the brakes on his reality TV career.

After more than two years of spotlighting the highs and lows of his and fiancée Kristen Doute's life on The Valley, the real estate agent is walking away from the Vanderpump Rules spinoff.

"I'll set the record straight," Doute told Page Six in an interview published Nov. 20. "Luke has decided not to film The Valley this season. It was a discussion that he and I had together, really just focusing on our family and Luke's mental health before we started production."

While she and Broderick—who share 16-month-old daughter Kaia—spoke at length about his choices for the show's future, she planned to support whatever decision he made.

"I really left it in his hands and said I would love for him to be a part of it, of course, but if it wasn't right for him," she explained, "then I wanted to be there to support that as well and that was the decision he made. So he gets to spend a lot more time with Kaia these days, which is wonderful."

The most recent season—which concluded in August—gave fans a front-row seat to the couple's relationship struggles, including sexual intimacy and communication, especially after welcoming Kaia.

"No secret, last season was very difficult for both of us," she added. "Two-and-a-half months after having Kaia, we started filming. I had a really difficult postpartum until Kaia was about 10 months old, and I think there was a lot of expectation versus reality as new parents that we didn't really know."

Although Bravo has yet to officially confirm a season four renewal, Broderick's exit is only the most recent cast shake-up. In fact, Danny Booko and Nia Sanchez are staying put in Santa Clarita.

"We're incredibly grateful for this experience," the couple announced on Instagram in September, "but our priority is protecting our peace and our family. We are fully committed to each other and our beautiful children."

Booko and Sanchez—parents to son Asher, 5, twins Isabelle and Zariah, 3, and Adelaide, 16 months—also raised a glass to their fans for all the love and support.

"We want to thank everyone for all the love and support you've shown us," the statement continued. "Thank you to Bravo and the team for everything. We are looking forward to what the next chapter brings."

As Doute and Broderick focus on the next chapter of their lives, keep reading for more unexpected TV show exits.

"You have a whole other life, Alex," he told her. "You got married. You have a beautiful daughter. And she needs you. That’s the life that you’re meant to live. You have to go back."

The couple announced that the third season of The Valley will be their last following a tumultuous season during which Danny’s drinking habits were questioned and he was accused of acting inappropriately while drinking.

#774. What history tells us about the Premier League table after 10 games of a season

Past years suggest it is tough to make big positional gains after slow start but that someone now safe will be relegated

The Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged.

Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38. Only 5.5 clubs per season moved by more than three places over the final 28 games, with almost half of the teams (89 out of 200) shifting by a single spot at most. Every club other than Arsenal will be looking to improve their position but they need not trouble themselves too much. History shows they will probably finish 2026-27 close to their current standing.

There have inevitably been outliers. Tottenham have tumbled by at least 10 places after matchweek 10 in the past two seasons and Newcastle (in 2021-22), Crystal Palace and Everton (both 2017-18) have risen from the relegation zone at this point to the safety of mid-table by May.

But even moving one position across the remainder of the season can make an enormous difference to a team on the fringe of the Champions League qualification spots, or to those that sit 17th or 18th after 10 games. Not since 2006-07 have the bottom three clubs with 28 matches to go all been relegated.

This fact feels especially relevant this season given two of the three teams in the drop zone have changed their manager since the previous round of matches. Sunderland have stood by Régis Le Bris but he is the favourite to be the next Premier League manager to leave their post. If we can reasonably assume at least one of the clubs currently 18th to 20th will be in the top flight in 2027-28, which is best placed to survive?

It is going to be very tough for Crystal Palace. Opta’s underlying data model implies they are where they deserve to be in the table, whereas Manchester United and Sunderland should be much higher. The largest improvement Palace’s new manager, Thomas Frank, engineered between weeks 10 and 38 at Brentford was two places, which will not cut it this season. Palace have to take inspiration from the 2024-25 season, in which they also had seven points after 10 games yet rose to finish 12th.

Mauricio Pochettino’s Chelsea were 11th going into their 11th game in 2023-24 before ending sixth. As they were also 11th in early April, they made a much shorter dash to the finish line, though. Pochettino’s teams usually improve as campaigns wear on, with Tottenham rising three places after week 10 in each of his first three seasons with the club. A similar lift in his new role would not make this season a rousing success for United but it would stave off the unthinkable idea of relegation.

For someone to escape, someone else must take their place. Ignoring the possibility that the answer to “who?” may be Manchester City, the team in 17th are inevitably the ones most at risk. Of the 13 sides in the past decade who were outside the drop zone after 10 games but went down, six were fourth-bottom going into matchweek 11.

Given that the points gap between first and 20th (20) was last lower at this stage in 2015-16, those figures may be more pertinent than position this season. Leeds in 2022-23 and Bournemouth three years earlier had 13 points after 10 games but were relegated, as did Blackpool in 2010-11 and Middlesbrough two seasons before them.

Only nine clubs are now above that bar, with Aston Villa, Newcastle and Tottenham among those who are not. The table is unlikely to change too much before the end of the campaign but there is a distinct chance that a secure-looking side will perish.

#772. Washington Spirit provide hope and joy in a city that badly needs it

Spirit’s run to the NWSL Championship final is in part based on a positive connection with fans at a time when DC is troubled in more ways than one

In the moments after the Washington Spirit’s 2-1 semi-final victory over the Utah Royals last weekend, all of Audi Field was in rapture. In the stands, around 20,000 Spirit supporters had filled the stadium to capacity, the sixth time they’d done so in 2026. They filled the place with the type of wondrous noise that’s become alien in DC sports in recent years, the type of gleeful adoration reserved for the city’s rare winners. The Spirit will return to their home stadium to face the Kansas City Current in the NWSL championship this Saturday.

In short order, the Spirit’s players made their way to the north end of the stadium, taking their celebrations into the crowd with their supporters. Perhaps no player has done more to push the Spirit into not only local but national relevance than US women’s national team forward Trinity Rodman, and Rodman herself grabbed a flag from a fan, jubilantly waving it above the crowd. Moments later, she bolted back onto the field and track down the club’s owner, Michele Kang, cajoling the businesswoman into a celebratory dance.

In the echo of all of this, many media members covering the match in the press box received an email from DC United, the local Major League Soccer club that operates and rents out Audi Field to the Spirit. It was a press release announcing the dismissal of their head coach, René Weiler. As the Spirit celebrated a third consecutive championship appearance on the pitch below, some unfortunate soul in a nearby office was tasked with sending that notice, the final nail in yet another dreadful season. While the women have thrived, the local men’s team has not made the playoffs in nearly a decade.

The Spirit, who share not only United’s stadium but also their training facility, are not asking to be compared to them. In reality no NWSL team is, as the audiences for men’s and women’s teams in the same city frequently prove to be quite different. Yet the differing fortunes of the two clubs and the stark difference in atmosphere at their games makes it nearly impossible not to do so. Once-mighty United, four-time MLS Cup champions, have become a laughingstock. That has not stopped the club’s ownership from seeking hundreds of millions of dollars from the DC government to renovate their eight-year-old stadium. While they lobby for that assistance, their matches have become borderline funerary affairs.

The Spirit? The club has become a beacon of hope and joy in a city that badly needs it. The District is a wildly diverse, deeply progressive place and its residents have struggled at times to come to terms with the political realities of hosting the current presidential administration. Thousands of National Guard troops roam the streets, more than a year into an anti-crime deployment that many believe hasn’t helped the city at all. In the shadow of all of this, Spirit matches have become a refuge. And while much of that relief comes from soccer the club plays – technical, entertaining – much of it comes from a deeper place.

“I think it’s the way that we bring the fans into everything that we do,” Rodman told the Guardian. “I think the way we interact with them after games, it’s not just a meet and greet. We truly do have conversations, and it feels like they’re our friends in a way. I think that’s amazing. The way that we celebrate, we’re always celebrating and interacting with them in the stadium - I feel like it’s a very safe, inclusive environment.

“There is always new people coming to each and every game and what I’ve heard is that everybody feels comfortable when they come to a game, there’s so many friends made. The comfort in it, the safety, the inclusivity of it at all.”

The Spirit have been mentioned as potential benefactors of United’s push for renovations at Audi Field, but Spirit ownership has long harbored bigger ambitions. The club have strong ties to the NFL’s Washington Commanders, who are moving into a new 65,000-seat home as part of a $4bn deal in the coming years, and “opportunities for women’s soccer” made up part of the pitch for that stadium’s public funding. Kang has spoken about aspirations of constructing a standalone training facility and moving the club out of the one it shares with United, a glorified collection of shipping containers in exurban Loudoun county, Virginia.

“I’m hoping in the future we do have that,” said Rodman. “Especially with how great we’ve done and how this organization is as a whole, that would be the cherry on top. Sharing facilities isn’t the greatest for anybody; to be able to have our own facilities with our own logos on it, our own space, not worried about timing would be great and I’m hoping it happens soon.”

All of it feels plausible. Should the Spirit remain competitive, and continue to endear to the District’s residents, it almost feels probable.

#771. Can the EU make it harder to trick consumers online?

The EU wants to curb subscription traps, misleading sales tactics and features that keep people scrolling. What would the proposed Digital Fairness Act change, and does it go far enough?

You sign up for a free trial to watch a series after work. A month later, you've forgotten about it. Then you find a charge for your new 12-month subscription on your bank statement. Sound familiar? You're not alone. Now the EU wants to stop that practice.

Under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a company would have to remind you before the free trial ends and get your explicit agreement before it can start charging you. The proposed law would also make it easier to cancel a subscription online and require reminders before certain contracts renew automatically.

The Commission presented the proposal on Wednesday. It wants to give consumers more control over how much time and money they spend online.

"We haven't seen that kind of reform in consumer protection in the last 20 years," Agustin Reyna, director general of the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), told DW.

His organization pushed for stronger EU rules against manipulative online practices. He sees the proposal as a good starting point for tackling problems that frustrate consumers every day.

The proposal also includes a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, so-called "dark patterns." A concrete example: You are trying to reserve a hotel room and the website claims that only three are left, a potentially false claim to pressure you into buying.

A concert ticket that gets more expensive while you're waiting in an online queue raises a different problem. The price could still go up in the process, but the seller would have to show the current price while you wait and tell you the maximum you could be asked to pay.

Online games that encourage users to spend their money to advance are also targeted. Children would no longer be able to pay to win or get to the next level of their online game.

Marketing and personalized ads would need to be clearly marked and restricted in the case of children. Consumers should get the option to switch off doomscrolling functions such as the autoplay of videos, showing one clip after the other. With these new rules, the EU wants to make apps and websites less addictive.

For Christoph Busch, an academic with a focus on consumer law and digital services based at Osnabrück University in Germany, the option to opt out doesn't go far enough. He argues that a version in which consumers actively have to choose to opt into those functions would be more effective.

"But then there is always the question of proportionality," Busch said. "And I think here the European legislators are trying to balance different interests."

These competing interests are particularly visible in the gaming industry, where interest groups have warned that the proposed EU restrictions could hurt developers and leave players with fewer options to choose from.

Video Games Europe and the European Games Developer Federation called the proposal "unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate," arguing that a ban on selling children features that help them win or advance is worded so broadly that it "could cover almost any purchase in a game."

For Busch, this argument doesn't hold. "If your business model is based on addictive design features, then maybe your business model has to be reviewed," he said.

Catalina Goanta, an associate professor of private law and technology at Utrecht University, emphasized in an interview with DW that "regulation can very easily slide into overregulation."

Even though she believes that the DFA is a solid and reasonable compromise, she argues that prohibiting dark patterns and doomscrolling altogether would be too prohibitive. Many of the issues consumers currently face could be resolved by enforcing existing regulation more effectively, she said.

She points to the fact that the EU has made a name for itself in the past by adding new rules and regulations that have made it more difficult to access the European market, especially for small online businesses.

"Instead of having 27 different regulations to adhere to, companies will now only get one," Reyna said.

For him, this speaks for simplification, especially when the responsibility for compliance is shared between online influencers and the platforms they publish on.

According to the new legislation, the EU would have the possibility to impose fines of up to six percent of a company's global annual revenue should the company violate the law.

The European Parliament and the Council, which represents member state governments, still have to agree on the text and formally adopt it. All experts agree that in that process, changes are still very likely.

"It will be a difficult trialogue, especially in this climate of simplification and deregulation with a focus on strengthening European competitiveness," said Christoph Busch. In that climate, it is not easy to add consumer rights, he adds.

Agustin Reyna is more optimistic. "The parliament is a divided house, much more than in the past," he says. "But consumer protection is a subject that brings parties together because it brings tangible outcomes to people."

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

So after desperately trying to break into either tears or just a smile at Harry Kane’s appearance record – no dice, unfortunately – here is a rundown on the state of play for each club, as we prepare for a weekend of football that might actually make us feel something.

1 Arsenal There are some genuinely likable things about the Gunners – Bukayo Saka, Paul Merson being a bit giddy, Ben White’s apathy to it all – but Arsenal fans were a lot easier to manage when they weren’t this good. It’s theirs to lose, etc.

3 Manchester City Enjoy it while it lasts, lads.

4 Liverpool These lot haven’t been title contenders since Mohamed Salah started playing like Robert Snodgrass and haven’t looked like vastly improving since replacing the right-winger with various different, expensive left-wingers.

13 Hull City A remarkable achievement that the promoted side are not anywhere near the bottom three considering there is absolutely nobody, including Sergej Jakirovic, who can name 11 current Hull players off the top of their heads.

14 Ipswich Town Shining bright like Gary O’Neil’s teeth. Keep this up and they might even survive.

#768. Why injured Joao Pedro may be Chelsea's most important player

Joao Pedro has scored five goals in six Premier League games this season

Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent absence has certainly strengthened the argument in his favour.

The debate started again among Blues fans over the past couple of weeks following their 1-0 defeat by Sunderland, the latest in a run of poor results without the Brazil striker.

The 25-year-old will miss Leeds United's visit on Saturday with a thigh injury after Chelsea lost three of their previous four matches without him, although one defeat came in a penalty shootout against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.

Having suffered a 2-0 home defeat by Tottenham in that run, manager Xabi Alonso has faced criticism over his side's lack of identity and some of his personnel decisions, particularly when attempting to replace Joao Pedro.

Danny Welbeck, who was expected to provide cover after his summer arrival from Brighton, has started only one Premier League match during Joao Pedro's injury absence.

Instead, Pedro Neto has twice been deployed through the middle, in the home win over Manchester United and the defeat by Sunderland, while Morgan Rogers started as the central striker against Spurs.

Striker Emmanuel Emegha, signed from Strasbourg over the summer, hasn't started a league game but has struggled with fitness issues of his own.

The continued absence of Joao Pedro is certainly proving costly before the busy winter schedule, with fifth-placed Chelsea already 11 points behind Premier League leaders Arsenal.

Having been handed both a new contract until 2034 and the number nine shirt vacated by Liam Delap in August, Chelsea regard their Â£55m signing from Brighton in 2025 as a key figure in Alonso's plans.

Asked about scoring more goals without the striker on Friday, Alonso said: "Yes, we need the whole team for that. It's not just the strikers who can score, we can score in set-pieces from defenders, midfielders, so it's teamwork for sure.

"Joao is an important player but we need to be this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.

"The other players, they need to step up and they need to show that they are ready to compete and ready to play for Chelsea."

There is little doubt Alonso has suffered when Joao Pedro has been unavailable, as did his predecessors. The numbers are undeniable.

Since the start of the 2025-26 Premier League season, Chelsea have averaged 1.8 goals per game with Joao Pedro, compared to 0.6 without.

Their expected goals (xG) drop from 1.8 per game with him to 1.1 without, highlighting a decline in Chelsea's attacking output rather than simply their finishing.

Chelsea average 4.8 shots on target per game when the Brazilian plays, compared with 3.9 when he does not.

Chelsea have failed to score in only 12.2% of Premier League matches involving him, compared with 71.4% when he has been absent.

Those numbers are also reflected in the results.

Chelsea have lost without scoring in just 7.3% of league games featuring Joao Pedro, compared with 71.4% without him. Three of their Premier League defeats this season were without him, while they have scored in every game that he has featured.

Chelsea's points-per-game average falls from 1.5 to 0.9 when he is unavailable.

Joao Pedro, who has also operated as a number 10 and on the wing for Chelsea, appears to improve the output of those around him.

During the past season and a half, Palmer has played 2,317 Premier League minutes alongside him and 528 without him.

Palmer has scored 12 goals and registered four assists with the Brazil forward in the side, equating to 0.6 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Without him, Palmer has managed one goal and no assists, equivalent to 0.2 goal involvements per 90.

Palmer's chance creation actually increases when Joao Pedro is absent, rising from 1.4 chances created per 90 minutes to 1.9. However, his goals return falls from 0.5 per 90 to 0.2, suggesting the striker's presence is more closely linked to Palmer's goalscoring output than his creativity.

The pair have developed a productive partnership. Joao Pedro has assisted four Palmer goals, while Palmer has provided three assists to the ex-Brighton forward..

There is less data available for Rogers given his more recent arrival, but the trend is similar.

Rogers has played 523 Premier League minutes alongside Joao Pedro and 360 without him. With Joao Pedro available, Rogers averages 0.7 goals per 90 minutes and 0.9 goal involvements per 90. Without him, those figures fall to 0.3 goal involvements per 90.

While the sample size remains relatively small, the figures suggest Chelsea's attacking players generally produce more when Joao Pedro plays.

All three of his assists this season have been for either Rogers or Palmer, sparking early season excitement about Chelsea's new trio, with nicknames like 'JP Morgan' and 'CPR' having been given to them.

With 20 goals and eight assists, Joao Pedro has been directly involved in 36.4% of Chelsea's 77 Premier League goals since joining the club.

Whether he is the Blues' most important player remains open to debate.

The statistics do show, however, that their points return with him in the side is consistent with Champions League qualification, whereas their return without him is not.

Alonso's team have yet to demonstrate they can perform at the same level when the Brazilian is unavailable.

#767. First defeat and first red for Ferguson as Glentoran falter

Ferguson was sent off in just his fourth game as Glentoran manager

It was a night of unfortunate firsts for Duncan Ferguson at Solitude on Friday.

The Everton great suffered his first defeat as Glentoran boss as they were edged out 3-2 by Cliftonville in an Irish Premiership thriller.

He also received his first red card as a manager, after picking up nine during his playing career, in the first half for protesting the decision to award Cliftonville's first goal after he perceived a foul in the build-up.

The defeat ended Glentoran's eight-game unbeaten run in the league and leaves them well off the pace in pursuit of their first league title since 2009.

While he has delivered with his animated touchline antics, Ferguson has so far struggled to get much out of his side on the pitch.

Ferguson sent off as Reds beat Glens in thriller - report and highlights

The Glens were second best for much of the first half in north Belfast, with Cliftonville dominating possession and creating the better chances.

Still, the awarding of the Reds' first goal was controversial as it looked like defender Jarlath O'Rourke had been pushed by Liam McStravick, who then teed up Joe Sheridan to score the opener on 38 minutes.

Ferguson was incensed that the goal stood, protesting while his side went up the other end and scored an equaliser through Cal Weatherup's deflected strike a minute later.

Such was the vehemence of his words towards the officials, referee Ben McMaster brandished a straight red card and Ferguson was forced to make the long walk to the tunnel all while being jeered by Cliftonville supporters.

"I think the manager got frustrated because it was a foul. It changes the dynamic [the sending off], he's a leader, I've then got to step in and fill his boots and it's a big set of boots to fill," said Ferguson's assistant Gary Bollan.

His side looked to have received a stern talking to from Bollan at half-time as they were much more competitive after the break.

They responded to Brian Healy putting the Reds ahead once again with a fine James Douglas strike on 86 minutes, which looked to be enough to secure a point and continue their unbeaten run.

However, they failed to stop midfielder Sheridan, who waltzed into the box before firing into the top corner two minutes later to seal a win.

Glentoran's fifth league defeat of the campaign leaves them 14 points behind pacesetters Linfield.

Former Crusaders captain Colin Coates, who was on co-commentary duties for the game for BBC Sport NI, believes Ferguson and the club have "a lot of work to do" to get back challenging for major honours.

"Look at the squad, there is work to do in January and next summer," he added.

"Duncan Ferguson will use this next few months to assess what he has, what he wants to keep and what he needs to bring in to make them competitive. Every time I watch them I want more from them.

"There is a real lack of quality particularly at the top end they don't look like they can hurt teams aside from Jordan Stewart. A lot of work and soul searching to do and players will be playing for their futures."

Stewart was suspended for the game at Solitude and was a big miss while Ferguson will hope to get more out of Conor McMenamin and the fit-again Pat Hoban, who both came on in the second half.

The Glens face two games against Larne, one in the BetMcLean Cup on Tuesday and one in the league next Friday and Ferguson will hope to mastermind two big results to really kick-start his reign.

Sheridan scored two fine goals in Cliftonville's victory

For Cliftonville, it was a case of another big performance under the lights on a Friday in front of a raucous Solitude crowd.

The Reds beat Larne 4-2 at the same venue a fortnight ago and key in their two big wins in recent weeks has been teenage midfielder Sheridan, who is growing in stature for Jim Magilton.

The 19-year-old broke into the senior squad last season after a fruitful six-month spell at Queen's University in the 2024-25 campaign.

He won the club's Young Player of the Year award last season and was a rotation option, but he has kicked on again this year and firmly established himself in a midfield three with captain Rory Hale and Dean McMaster.

The next step for the talented Northern Ireland under-21 international is adding goals and assists to his game and he certainly delivered on Friday.

Former Glentoran captain Paul Leeman said he showed "composure" for both his goals, first to curl home from close range, then to weave his way into the box and place the ball in the top corner.

"It was a really good performance from him. He's becoming a mainstay in the team," Leeman added.

The victory moves Cliftonville to within a point of the Glens and with games against struggling Ballymena United and Bangor to come, they will hope to embark upon another winning run to continue their surge up the table.

#766. Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet

The 30-year-old former England star combines Twitch streaming with working to return to the top as a player

Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.

“We’ll do maybe two days on, one day off, and then three days on, one day off,” says Peters. “We’ve been doing that for just over a year now. It’s full-on. It’s pretty much as if you were at a club.”

Dele rose as a teenager to a level of stardom few experience and, used to media attention, doesn’t mind that his absence from football draws scrutiny. But he disagrees with the suggestion that choosing to stream on Twitch is a sign he has lost interest in the game that made him wealthy enough to never need to work again.

To a modest Twitch audience, he sometimes plays video games, sometimes just talks. He has a knack for creating viral content, sharing a phone call with Harry Kane and playing a game of EA Sports FC with IShowSpeed, one of the most famous online influencers. When he lost that game – and a bet – he wore an Arsenal shirt, apologising to Spurs fans before burning it. When TalkSport pundits claimed Dele was wasting his potential by becoming a streamer, Dele responded in a live stream, pointing out he was recording himself in his spare time and if he was out at nightclubs, it would be worse. Even then he was polite.

“When people see him online streaming or whatever he does in his private time, the initial thought is: ‘He’s done with football, then,’” Peters says. “He’s been training for a year and a half by himself. If he was done with football he wouldn’t be doing that. His actions show that the hunger is still there. A lot of people would come out of the game and then stop and lose the hunger for it, but he’s still chipping away every day, trying to get back and get to somewhere that he’s happy with.”

Dele broke through at MK Dons as a slight but devilish defensive midfielder, dominating League One midfields full of hardened professionals, before being scouted by Tottenham. Mauricio Pochettino attended MK Dons’ 4-0 League Cup win against Manchester United in 2014 and saw enough to leave early and convince Daniel Levy to pay £5m.

By the time Dele turned 21, his statistics were superior to Cristiano Ronaldo’s at the same age: 26 goals and 14 assists to Ronaldo’s 14 and 13. His 40 goal involvements equalled Frank Lampard, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham combined at the same age.

“He’s scored more in his first 50 league games than Steven Gerrard, Wayne Rooney and Frank Lampard,” Pochettino wrote in his book Brave New World. “He may go on to be better than all of them because he has the quality; now he just needs consistency.”

But there were, perhaps, warning signs of what would happen at Spurs. One source who worked closely with Dele describes him as a “cheeky chappy”; charming and universally popular.

He wasn’t one to miss training, but there were concerns he wasn’t leading the pristine lifestyle of many elite players, and tabloid stories about his private life trailed him. Pochettino was concerned when he saw Dele’s WhatsApp photo, a cartoon of a boy surrounded by people wanting a piece of him, believing he needed support from the right people. John McDermott, the head of coaching and development, said: “When the trough is full, the pigs come from all over to feed.”

When Dele voluntarily liquidated one of his companies this month, documents showed an estimated surplus after costs of £7.6m, suggesting the 30-year-old has not squandered the millions he earned at his peak in wages and sponsorship agreements, including a five-year deal with Adidas. He also owns a property portfolio worth more than £1.5m.

In the early days Pochettino warned Dele about the danger of not giving maximum effort in matches and training, a sentiment later shared by José Mourinho when he became Spurs manager. “I think one day you will regret, if you don’t reach what you can reach,” Mourinho told Dele in his office as Amazon Prime’s cameras rolled.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although Dele formed a formidable relationship with Kane on the pitch, and was twice named the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s young player of the year while playing behind the striker, he was closer to Eric Dier off it. And perhaps it was those anchors – Pochettino and Dier – that Dele lost later in his career.

His time with Pochettino was fondly remembered. For the Argentinian’s 50th birthday celebrations, Dele recorded a heartfelt video for his former manager. “The message was beautiful,” says one party-goer.

In almost five years since leaving Spurs, he has made one league start at Everton and 10 at Besiktas, before a loan at Como, where Cesc Fàbregas tried to rediscover the player he once was. He came off the bench once and was sent off nine minutes later.

Dele, according to those close to him, is biding his time to get his next move right. He will be 31 in April and wants a suitable contract. He has spoken to a host of clubs, with interest from the Premier League and the Championship, and from the Middle East, where he has been tempted by the riches of the Saudi Pro League, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. There has also been interest from Major League Soccer and he has held talks with clubs in Brazil and Japan. It is believed he will join a club this season.

In preparation, Peters is also guiding Dele’s nutrition, though he does not require much guidance. “Del’s a weird one, because he doesn’t snack, he doesn’t eat unhealthily, he doesn’t have a Sprite or a Coke or whatever. He’s never really been that kind of guy. All he does is drink coconut water, and he’ll have a small lunch, or his cheat day will be a Nando’s or something.”

Happiness is his priority. He spoke candidly on Gary Neville’s The Overlap in 2023 about his struggles with mental health and an addiction to sleeping pills after revealing abuse as a child. “Because he’s had such a long time out, he’s like: ‘What’s another few months if it means that I’m going to find something I’m actually happy with?’” Peters says. The aim is to “carry on for as long as possible”.

For the time being, Dele’s days are simple. When not training, he goes for coffee or a swim, and he has taken up padel. “He’s very much a person that’s happy with the little things,” Peters says. “He’s always the person that’s positive, the one that, if the group’s down or whatever, is going to pick everyone up. He’s happy with what he’s doing. His main happiness is playing football, and that’s what he wants to do.”

#765. EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

A seat at the table for Europe now appears likely following comments by a US envoy who just held talks with Putin. But who will take that seat remains unclear.

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.

"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.

But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.

Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.

"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."

Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.

"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.

European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.

Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.

"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."

This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.

"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."

Zelensky said he found the US approach "a bit strange."

Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.

They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.

The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.

Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.

Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.

But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.

#764. Chelsea fined £150,000 for discriminatory chanting

Chelsea have been fined Â£150,000 by the Football Association as part of a punishment for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants during an FA Cup third-round win at Charlton Athletic in January.

The club have also been warned about their future conduct and had an action plan imposed on them in relation to the offence.

"Chelsea FC failed to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief," said an FA statement., external

Chelsea admitted the charge but had an appeal against the fine issued by an independent regulatory commission rejected.

The FA's written reasons stated that although the discriminatory chanting "lasted approximately one minute and was not repeated, the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".

"We unequivocally condemn this behaviour," said a Chelsea statement., external "Sectarian abuse - chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group - and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.

"Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary."

The FA itself was fined by Uefa for a similar incident of chanting, from England's away support during their Nations League victory in Spain on Sunday.

#763. 10 games, 0 points & 30 goals conceded - why Charlton are struggling

Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer

Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.

After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.

They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.

The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.

"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills said following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.

That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.

So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?

Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.

An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.

However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.

Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).

They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.

The only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.

Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.

"I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.

"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.

"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward."

This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.

Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.

"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.

"It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?"

Whitehouse's penalty masterclass sends Charlton into WSL

How WSL 2 title contenders Charlton are defying the odds

Karen Hills was a player at Charlton Athletic before retiring in 2007

Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.

It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.

Charlotte Newsham, who played a key role in their WSL 2 promotion run, was also sidelined by an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury before the play-off victory.

While Charlton sought out shrewd signings in the summer, rivals Birmingham City were able to spend six-figure sums on Manchester United duo Lisa Naalsund and Millie Turner.

The Blues also broke their club record in January - a reported Â£316,000 fee for Wilma Leidhammar - while Oceane Hurtre was signed last summer to boost their second-tier title hopes and has now scored seven goals in 10 WSL games.

Fellow promoted club Palace picked up four-time WSL winner Bethany England and one of the WSL 2's standout players Lexi Lloyd-Smith in the summer.

"WSL 2 teams have to be even more ready for the WSL while they're still in the WSL 2 so that when they do make that jump, it's not a huge gap," said Hills.

"The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see some of the players the top teams have brought in and the finances they have.

"It's a big challenge for us. We're finding that out on a weekly basis."

Charlton benefited from the WSL's expansion this summer to 14 teams from 12 as organisers try to bridge the gap between the leagues and to increase the number of matches.

It was well-received by fans and those within the game, but Hills says it will still take time for WSL 2 clubs to catch up.

"If you look at the bottom three teams [in the table], it's all the newly-promoted teams. The level that we're coming into is already very well established."

Neville added: "I think the financial side plays a massive part. We do our bit where we can. But it's hard to bring in the experienced players you need."

#762. Tom Brady in talks over buying Chelsea stake after Birmingham City exit

NFL legend was Chelsea guest at Club World Cup

Brady has good relationship with Behdad Eghbali

Tom Brady is in discussions about buying a small stake in Chelsea. The NFL legend sold a minority share in Birmingham City this month after three years, a move sources said was to pave the way for investing at Stamford Bridge.

Brady was a guest of Chelsea when they won the Club World Cup in New Jersey last year and was seen celebrating with the players after their remarkable 3-0 final win over Paris Saint-Germain.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner is understood to have a good relationship with Behdad Eghbali, whose fund, Clearlake Capital, owns 86.5% of Chelsea after Todd Boehly and Mark Walter sold their shares in September.

Brady bought into Birmingham in August 2023, less than a year after his second and final retirement from the NFL, after the club’s takeover by Tom Wagner’s Knighthead Capital.

Brady was appointed chair of the club’s advisory board and had a prominent role in the 2025 Amazon Prime documentary Built in Birmingham: Brady & The Blues, which made headlines when he questioned the “work ethic” of Wayne Rooney, who was the manager.

In announcing Brady’s departure the club said: “Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.”

Brady owns a minority stake in the NFL team Las Vegas Raiders, which he purchased alongside Wagner.

#761. Filming training by drones should be illegal - Iraola

Andoni Iraola's Liverpool take on Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United on Sunday

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.

Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.

The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.

Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.

"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.

"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.

"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

Filming training on a drone 'shouldn't be legal' - Iraola

Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match.

"We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola.

"We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."

Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday.

"They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said.

"Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."

Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.

But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign.

"You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games.

"We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways.

"We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."
