STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.

Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did.

Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench.

The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies.

Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II, with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away.

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space, while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase.

That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase.

Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball.

This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system.

Ship continued on to low Earth orbit, where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites. It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX says is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite launches worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation.

Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch.

At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower.

After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight.

It hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts.

SpaceX has not yet said whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry.

Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

#731. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

#730. Emmy Rossum on Producing and Starring in ‘Furious’: “I Have Been ‘Matrix’-Style Dodging Mega-Predators Since I Was Seven”

In front of an audience at the Newport Beach Film Festival, the actress reflects on her breakthrough in 'The Phantom of the Opera,' her quest for equal pay on 'Shameless' and her production company: "I like characters that are living in moral gray areas. That's something that I wasn't really able to do in the ingenue years."

“I have been Matrix-style dodging mega-predators since I was seven years old,” actress-producer Emmy Rossum said during a recording of The Hollywood Reporter’s Awards Chatter podcast at the recent Newport Beach Film Festival, where she was being honored with the fest’s Outstanding Performance in Television Award for her work on Hulu’s Furious. The drama series, which she also produced, tells a cat-and-mouse tale of a female FBI agent (Rossum) and a young female serial killer (Lola Petticrew), both PTSD-afflicted survivors of sexual abuse. “So,” Rossum continued, “I firsthand understand the nuance and complexity of being a young person in situations like this and of being a powerful professional woman in situations like this.” Related Stories 'Awards Chatter' Podcast Jessica Lange on Bringing 'Long Day's Journey Into Night' Back to the Big Screen, Returning to 'American Horror Story' and Retirement Rumors News Emmy Rossum Named RAINN Ambassador Amid New Partnership to Deepen Public Understanding of Sexual Violence and Survivorship (Exclusive)

Rossum, who was once described by the late Roger Ebert as “a phenomenal talent,” is only 40, but she has been doing outstanding work for nearly 30 years — in films like 2000s Songcatcher, 2003’s Mystic River, 2004’s The Phantom of the Opera and 2013’s Beautiful Creatures; TV limited series such as Angelyne (2022) and The Crowded Room (2023); and, of course, for 110 episodes over nine seasons on the TV series Shameless (2011-2019), several episodes of which she also directed.

As Rossum’s time on Shameless came to an end, she launched a production company, Composition 8, which she now runs with Sara Moskowitz and Sam Russell. Their first project was Angelyne, in which Rossum played the eponymous Los Angeles billboard queen. They have since made several others. Rossum explains, “The throughline in things that I’ve been looking for is: I like characters that are living in moral gray areas. That’s something that I wasn’t really able to do in the ingenue years.”

But obtaining choice material is not easy for a small company, even one run by a top young actress. “We have to be scrappy because we’re not LuckyChap [Margot Robbie’s company], and we’re not Hello Sunshine [Reese Witherspoon’s company],” she explains. “We’re three people with this mandate of wanting to tell complicated stories about women that talk about something in the zeitgeist and culture and where we are now — and make really entertaining and fun stuff.”

What led them to Furious, their most successful project yet? Rossum recounts, “I was like, ‘OK, well, we’re not going to land any of the hot books, so where do we go look? We have to look where other people are not looking. Let’s look at all of the old movies that nobody’s looking at. Like, they were good, so why aren’t we looking there? There’s got to be one that’s got a good skeleton that we can uncover and figure it out.'”

That led them to Bob Rafelson’s 1987 cult classic Black Widow, which starred Debra Winger and Theresa Russell as an FBI agent and serial killer, respectively. The material was nearly 40 years old, but still “feels kind of contemporary,” she felt, noting eerie parallels with everything from the Jeffrey Epstein saga to the “Jane Doe” case at Cornell. So Composition 8 obtained the rights and set about putting it together. Rossum sold the show to Hulu via a text, recruited Liz Meriwether (The Dropout) to serve as showrunner and set about preparing to play cop-turned-FBI agent Alice Black, meeting with and shadowing law enforcement officials, consulting psychotherapists, adding considerable muscle to her small physique and more.

She reflects, “It’s interesting to play a character who can hold so many complexities, who can be infinitely, bottomlessly vulnerable and terrified and afraid to be weak at the same time as being incredibly manipulative and physically and emotionally powerful and dogged and smart and underestimated. It was the role that haunted me the most, and it was a benefit that I came on so early, because I felt that I was working on the character for three years before we started shooting.”

The first season of Furious, which rolled out in July and August, was described by The New York Times as “remarkable.” Rossum’s part, meanwhile, was described by The Guardian as “the role of her life.” For it, she is now in serious contention for end-of-the-year honors — best actress in a drama series Critics Choice, Golden Globe and Actor Awards — and, next year, she might well become the first person with the name Emmy to, well, win one.

In the meantime, though, she’s headed back to work: a second season of Furious was ordered just before its season one finale aired, and it starts shooting in January. She can’t wait — but she also wants the industry to know that she’s not only interested in acting in stuff that she also produces: “I’m still in the incoming-call business, so please hire me! I want great roles.”

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

"Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."

Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

"For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn."

For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or New York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies plan to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

#727. “The Secrecy Was Insane:” The Making of ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ From Locked Safes to Original Cast’s Return

Screenwriter Billy Ray, producer Nina Jacobson and director Francis Lawrence reveal how they adapted Suzanne Collins’ prequel before it was published, found their young Haymitch and brought back Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson.

Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

Before the odds could be in their favor, the creative team behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had to survive a Games of their own, one played entirely in secret.

The rules were simple: one copy of the book, no internet and not a word to anyone. Related Stories Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Hunts Down $21M in Box Office Previews Movies Jennifer Lawrence Thinks Her 'Hunger Games' Bow and Arrow Prop Was Stolen

When Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins called her trusted adapters, director Francis Lawrence, producer Nina Jacobson and original Hunger Games screenwriter Billy Ray, they were eager to read her new story. The catch: it wasn’t fully finished, and it hadn’t been announced to the public. That meant caution was essential.

Take Ray’s process for example. The screenwriter didn’t write his latest Hunger Games script on his own computer. Each day, he drove onto the Fox lot to Jacobson’s office and sat down in a small room with a safe that guarded Collins’ story. An assistant opened the safe, took out a laptop that had never been connected to the internet and set it in front of him. He wrote all day, said “Done,” and the laptop went back into the safe.

“That’s how the script got written, which of course I had never done before,” Ray tells The Hollywood Reporter.

It was an unusual way to adapt a novel that almost no one outside that small circle knew existed, yet maintaining strict confidentiality was imperative given the phenomenon Collins’ franchise has become. The original four films — The Hunger Games, Catching Fire and Mockingjay Part 1 and 2 — grossed roughly $2.98 billion worldwide. Debuting with its first book in 2008, the dystopian saga following teenagers forced into fatal combat has grown into one of the most successful young adult publishing franchises in history. Across its five installments, the series has sold more than 100 million copies globally.

In 2020, Collins released her first prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, which chronicled the rise of the tyrant Coriolanus Snow. The film was adapted for feature film starring Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler. Now with Sunrise on the Reaping, released on Nov. 20, Collins has returned to another familiar face: Haymitch Abernathy, the District 12 mentor Woody Harrelson played in the films.

The prequel revisits the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, starting on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, when a younger Haymitch (portrayed by Joseph Zada) competes. Sunrise on the Reaping opens on Haymitch’s 16th birthday, which coincides with the second Quarter Quell, where the traditional choice of one male and one female from a district has been doubled to two of each.

Though initially not among the four selected tributes for District 12, Haymitch is automatically volunteered as punishment for trying to protect his girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) who reacts after one of the chosen boys tries to make a run for it and is shot by Capitol soldiers known as “Peacekeepers.”

The Haymitch origin story answers a question fans have had since the first film: how the hopeful, mischievous kid became the bitter, drunken mentor to Jennifer Lawrence‘s Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson‘s Peeta Mellark that Harrelson played.

Ahead of the film’s release, Ray, Jacobson and director Francis Lawrence spoke with THR about working under an NDA bubble, finding their new Haymitch and reuniting franchise alums Harrelson, Lawrence and Hutcherson.

When The Hunger Games was first adapted for the screen, screenwriter Ray and director Gary Ross launched what would grow into a global success. Since both Ray and Ross parted ways with the franchise following the initial installment, Ray’s comeback to craft the backstory for a character he helped popularize represented a complete full-circle experience.

“Having launched that franchise, The Hunger Games has been such a blessing in my career,” Ray tells THR. “I can’t begin to enumerate all the ways it’s been great for me.”

“When the opportunity came to come back, I said yes before I read the book,” he says of his return. “It was something I wanted to do. I wanted to work with Francis, and I wanted to be back under the hood with Suzanne and with Nina.”

Ray has stayed close with Collins, who read an early draft of his debut novel, Burn the Water, which was released earlier this year. “It was as if we had spoken the day before,” he says of reteaming with Collins and others for Sunrise on the Reaping. “There was just no falloff at all.”

When Collins calls, producer Jacobson, director Lawrence and Ray answer, ready to find out what the author has created this time. But her first question is always the same: “Why don’t you guys take a look and let me know if you think it’s a movie?”

“This is always kind of hilarious… We read this one and said, ‘Yeah, it’s a movie, Suzanne,'” Lawrence says, laughing. Jacobson’s answer was just as immediate: “My first response was, ‘Hell yes.'”

Collins’ question is a sincere one, though, Lawrence explains. “She’s very serious when she says it’s OK to tell her it’s not a movie. When you create anything, you’re vulnerable, and when she hands something to us, it’s usually not completely finished. She feels vulnerable about it and wants some reassurance that it really is worthy of being on the screen.”

Getting that far took some doing. When the team read an early draft of The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, the world was in lockdown, so keeping it secret was easier, Lawrence says. Sunrise on the Reaping brought “a different kind of tension, because the book had not yet been published, so the secrecy and security around the project was pretty extreme,” Ray says.

“For us, the secrecy was insane,” Jacobson says. “We had one hard copy of the book. It had to be mailed or messengered from New York to L.A. in sections. First it lived at her [Collins’] agent’s house and then eventually we got a safe for my office and it moved into the safe. There was one copy, and people could make an appointment if they needed to read it.”

The secrecy extended to casting, too. “Even once we had our script, we couldn’t release sides, or even use a scene from the book instead of sides, because if we read an actor, people would know what scenes and characters were in the book besides Haymitch,” Jacobson says. “So we had the young actors do improvs, just so we could get acquainted with this generation of actors and start to collect knowledge about who they are.”

“Having to keep it locked down in this NDA bubble was exciting,” she adds. “It was sort of stressful, and I was incredibly relieved when we could finally talk about it!”

“We knew Haymitch was going to be the trickiest person to cast, because we’re anchored with him,” Lawrence says.

Joseph Zada, who starred in Prime Video’s We Were Liars and had filmed Netflix’s East of Eden series, caught the attention of casting directors Debra Zane and Dylan Jury, who wanted Lawrence and Jacobson to meet him.

“He had sent in an improv tape. We had many, many people do improv tapes just to see who was out in the world, and his was pretty special,” Lawrence recalls.

From there, the audition process became its own Hunger Games. “We really put him through the wringer in the audition process,” the director admits. “We tested and tested to make sure he would be emotionally capable of going through everything he needed to go through, that he had the sense of mischief and irreverence Woody has, and that he could embody all those characteristics without feeling like he was doing an impression. That was the tricky thing. But he was definitely the guy.”

“We needed to know he had the range to experience all of the loss in the movie, and to do it in different ways: sometimes shame, guilt or anger, or just complete loss and grief,” Lawrence adds. “We needed somebody who could bring all of that.”

For Jacobson, the deciding quality was mischief. “You needed somebody who had mischief in them, and that’s a surprisingly hard thing to find,” she says. “There are some wonderful, likable actors who are very capable leading men, but who don’t necessarily have that mischief in them, that troublemaker vibe. And yet at his young age, it can’t be that dark, twisted kind of mischief-maker or trickster. It’s a boyish quality.”

Zada was someone who “had a hopeful, sunny disposition” and the mischief they wanted Haymitch to embody.

“When you first meet him in the original movies, you don’t understand why he’s so angry, drunken, broken and bitter. You assume, well, it can’t be easy being a mentor for the poorest, most disadvantaged district out there,” she continues. “What all of us wanted to see in this one, and what Joseph captured so beautifully, is that he was bright, funny, hopeful and very apolitical.”

Zada’s chemistry with Peak, cast as his love interest, Lenore Dove, sealed it. “You just felt it. You felt like this woman is the woman he loves. She’s his best friend. She’s the person who makes it all make sense for him,” Jacobson says of their chemistry reads together.

“There’s a quality about Woody, and we had to find someone who had that quality but wasn’t going to get burdened by it,” she says. “With all of our actors, we always said, ‘We don’t want impersonation. We want interpretation.'”

That philosophy extended well beyond Haymitch. From Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning to Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons and Ralph Fiennes, Sunrise wasn’t short on A-listers joining its younger, newer cast members that also included Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang, Molly McCann and Percy Daggs IV.

But joining an established franchise isn’t always an immediate yes, Jacobson says. “There are definitely some people who just don’t know the series that well, so it’s about educating them about it, and making sure they know we’re not looking for them to impersonate,” she explains. “We want their interpretation of the character. If they don’t know the series, oftentimes they have to go ask around a bit and talk to people in their lives.”

Culkin and Fanning, who play Caesar Flickerman and Effie Trinket, have been candid about finding their own interpretations while respecting the characters Stanley Tucci and Elizabeth Banks originated.

“What we tell people who are new to it, and I really do believe this quite earnestly, is that it’s one of the very few franchises where, for each of the renowned actors we cast, it is actually all about performance. It’s never about prosthetics or visual effects,” Jacobson says. (Well, almost never: “Of course we use those things sparingly here and there. Those are not Glenn’s teeth,” she notes.)

The appeal, she says, is the creative freedom that comes with everything being “rooted in performance.” “You’re going to be collaborating closely with Francis and the department heads on the creation, building and design of your character, and it’s going to come down to meaty character work. You’re very rarely against a green screen. You’re almost always in a practical location with, hopefully, some other amazing actors in the scenes with you. I think these movies give each actor a real showcase of their talents, in a way that isn’t always true in a lot of other franchises.”

Jacobson recalls Sunrise on the Reaping being an “incredibly emotional” read. “I cried quite a few times, and then cried quite a lot at the end. I found it so fully moving and satisfying on so many levels.”

But how do you adapt a book fans haven’t been able to read yet? The creative team relied on being fans themselves.

“Nina and I consider ourselves fans, so there are a lot of things we fight to keep from the book, details we love ourselves,” Lawrence says. “And Suzanne is obviously going to fight for certain things: making sure her themes, ideas, the spirit of the characters and their emotional arcs are there. So there’s a good group of us there to protect what we think fans are going to love.”

“The funny thing is, it’s incredibly easy for me to know how fans will feel, because I’m the OG fan,” Jacobson says. “I’m as obsessed with the books as any diehard fan, and so is Francis.”

Still, some things had to go. “If I put everything that’s in the book into the movie, the movie would be six hours long. You can’t do that,” Ray says.

Sunrise doubles the number of tributes competing in the Games, and the team knew they couldn’t explore every one in depth. “Getting to know the tributes and understanding potential allies and enemies is one of the parts of these movies people really enjoy and are invested in. So figuring out how to balance the 48, and making sure we gave time and attention to the core characters whose stories are connected to Haymitch’s journey, was a definite challenge,” Jacobson says.

The book is also told entirely from Haymitch’s point of view, which posed its own challenge. “What we found even in the original movies with Katniss was that if she wasn’t in a scene, the scene still needed to be about her in some way,” Jacobson says. “But when you’re only ever with that one person, there’s important context and opportunities you might miss. So figuring out where to break with his point of view, when to show something he can’t see or know, was a big decision in the adaptation process.”

As for every other decision, the guiding principle was Collins.

“At the very beginning of the process, I asked Suzanne, ‘What is this book about for you?'” Ray recalls. “She talked about the philosophy of the book: the philosophy of propaganda and implicit submission, the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, David Hume and John Locke. And I said, ‘Suzanne, what’s the book about for you emotionally?’ She said, ‘It’s about love and loss.’ I said, ‘Great, that’s what I’m writing.’ So anything that didn’t stick to that had to go.”

The Haymitch audiences meet in Sunrise is a far cry from the broken alcoholic of the original films. In Sunrise, audiences encounter a teen initially easygoing and unconcerned with politics. But his life transforms when he is forced into the 50th Hunger Games. Refusing to simply comply, he attempts to disrupt the Capitol’s system and oppose President Snow, altering both his own destiny and the world around him.

Jacobson likens the young Haymitch to the “kind of guy who’s probably not very serious about school and is just waiting for the end of the day to run down to the beach with his surfboard and his girlfriend, hang out and catch some waves.” His attitude, as she sees it: “I can’t do anything about this broken world that I live in, but I’ve got a girl I love and a family I love, and that’s enough for me. Who am I? What difference would I make anyway?”

Jacobson sees Haymitch’s arc as similar to Katniss’, with a priority on family that grows to include their community and district. “Your circle of concern grows in each movie, and there’s a cost to expanding that circle, a price to pay… But it’s the things he hears and brings with him from Lenore Dove. He says the Capitol has all the power and always will, and she says that doesn’t mean they always have, and it doesn’t mean they always will. It’s this notion that it’s not a foregone conclusion that oppressive power structures can’t be disrupted and ultimately destroyed.”

The Haymitch of the film faces a dilemma: “What am I willing to give up for the people I care about? And what am I willing to give up to right these really profound wrongs and try to end the Games?”

“Seeing him get radicalized, and seeing him decide, even with all this loss, that the way to honor these people is to continue to fight: that was what was really important to me, and what I found really interesting and moving,” Lawrence says.

“You see Haymitch in the other movies, and Woody does an amazing job portraying him, but people laugh with him,” the director adds. “He’s a drunk, and you just don’t know the history. Now you follow this movie and see all that he went through, how long and hard he fought, all the years he had to escort tributes to the arena and watch them die. But he continued to fight and kept his promise to his girlfriend, his mother, his brother, to Maysilee (portrayed by Grace) and all of them.”

For Ray, filling in that history was the point. “In that first movie, obviously Haymitch is just broken, with a real serious drinking problem and a lot of pain. This was the movie that explained all that, and it was great to do that sort of history retroactively, to say, ‘This explains the behavior you’ve been seeing through all those movies,'” he says. “People know what happened, and the trick is saying, ‘Here’s the part you didn’t know.’ That’s what we were going for here.”

Collins doesn’t write unless she has something to say, and themes have been the foundation of each Hunger Games book. With the original trilogy, she explored the consequences of war for teens. With the prequels, she continues to examine the state of the world.

“Look at the themes she’s dealing with now and how relevant they are: there’s a bit of a call to action, this idea of implicit submission, and diving into the use of propaganda to get people to submit. So there are fresh ideas that feel very relevant. There’s meat on the bone,” Lawrence says. “Take this idea of implicit submission. You can look at any government, whether it’s authoritarian, fascist or one that calls itself democratic: as humans, we always agree to be ruled by the few. It’s a bit of a call to action: don’t be apathetic, stand up, voice your beliefs, and don’t expect instant gratification, because change may take time. I feel that’s very relevant now, but it’s also timeless, because people are constantly fighting for their rights. You see it in Hungary, with the ousting of a regime, and in Brazil, where people actually make change. That’s happening now, but it’s also something that’s been happening for thousands of years.”

Ray says he approached both the original film and Sunrise as if they were “true stories.”

“And they’re getting closer and closer to being that, which is the bad news for us as a culture, and the great news for Suzanne Collins, because she has her finger on the pulse of something, and it does feel like a true story. If you think of it that way, you can write it as a screenwriter from a place of complete outrage,” he says.

Haymitch’s journey matters now even more given it’s “a time when so many people feel like, ‘What’s the point of trying to make a difference?'” Jacobson says. “It’s a story that is so emotional about how hard it is to try to make a difference. It’s also about how what you set in motion today might not be realized for another generation, and how hard it is to continue to resist and to endure, knowing that the changes you hope for could take 25 years to accomplish.”

Anyone who knows The Hunger Games knows the brutality of the story. “I think an audience that has bought into the concept that a government forces children to kill each other knows they’re coming to see something dark,” Ray says. “I don’t think anybody is going to come away saying, ‘Wow, I was expecting a musical. What the hell is this?'”

Even so, certain sequences in Sunrise had to be toned down to keep the film’s PG-13 rating.

“There’s a moment in the book where a character is holding the head of a child, and I thought, ‘We’re never going to be able to do that.’ There were probably three moments in the book where I went, ‘Come on, Suzanne, this is never going to happen.’ And she understands that when we get into the process,” Lawrence says.

The story’s emotional darkness stayed intact, and Lawrence says it was “toughest” on Zada, who had to ride that roller coaster on set.

“Whenever we led up to certain days, whether it was a Lenore Dove scene or a Maysilee scene, it was always a little scary for him, because he knew he’d have to sit in those feelings for 10 or 12 hours, basically all day,” he says.

The Games were filmed first, with the District 12 scenes shot later. “He was so happy to just be happy: going to work convinced he’d never get called in the reaping, having a nice scene in the meadow with Lenore Dove, being in the candy shop. He looked forward to those days,” Lawrence says.

But the darker turns were never far off. “We also had to do things like shoot his and Lenore Dove’s first scene one day and then, because we were in that location, jump to the end the very next day and do that whole scene (readers know the one.) That was tough on Joe. Even when he was happy to be happy, he knew what was coming tomorrow. That weighed on him more than it did on me,” the director says.

Though the book and film follow a younger Haymitch, the book’s epilogue, featuring Katniss, Peeta and an older Haymitch, was in the script from the start. “It was such a profound honor to get to write those characters again. It was just pure joy,” Ray says.

“I remember reading the epilogue in the manuscript and thinking, ‘Wow, this is fantastic.’ I found it really moving,” Lawrence says of the trio’s return in the book.

“The hope was always to bring them back,” the director says of Harrelson, Hutcherson and Jennifer Lawrence. But because of the secrecy surrounding the book and the adaptation, “We didn’t reach out to them until, I want to say, the day before the announcement. That’s when I called the three of them.”

While the team hoped for an immediate yes, they prepared in case scheduling conflicts or other circumstances kept the actors from returning. “We had already tasked ourselves with figuring out how to make the story as fulfilling as possible if it didn’t happen,” Lawrence says.

But there was no need to rethink the epilogue: the actors were “all very excited to return,” he says. “Then it was really just a scheduling question: when can we get the three of them together and out to Germany?” the director says.

Francis Lawrence has stayed in touch with the cast, but working together again in the world of The Hunger Games made for an especially meaningful reunion. “I think it was a Wednesday night when they arrived, and I got a text from Jen that she and Josh were having a beer in the hotel bar. I was coming back from set, so I joined, then Nina joined, and our cinematographer, the still photographer, the sound mixer… It’s the same group of people who have been making these movies for 16 years, so we had this great reunion of about 30 of us before costume fittings and all of that.”

With two prequel novels and films now out, the question is always whether there are more stories to tell in Panem. The creative team admits they’re just as in the dark as everyone else.

“She only really writes when she has something to say, so I hope she has something she wants to write about in this world, because I would miss it a lot,” Jacobson says.

Fans have been quick to name the characters they’d love to follow in their early years, with Finnick (portrayed by Sam Claflin) and Johanna (Jena Malone) at the top of the list, along with the first Hunger Games. After Sunrise, Jacobson’s own fascination is Plutarch. “When I realized from this book that Plutarch has been playing a double agent for 25 years by the time you meet him in Catching Fire, that to me is pretty fascinating. How do you pull that off? How could you possibly live that close to such danger? And what compromises did you have to make? He is not a morally clean character at all, so I have a total fascination with him,” she says.

If the prequels have proved anything, it’s to never say never, a lesson Jacobson says the team learned early. “When we finished the original trilogy of books, we really thought we were done. We’ve never tried to make a movie without a book of hers. We only make her books. We never tried to develop anything that wasn’t based on something she had given us as a book she was going to publish. So when we first got Ballad, all of a sudden it was, ‘Oh my god, we’re coming back to this world.'”

“I was so wowed by the way she’s taken us on this journey, and by the amount of things that come together in this movie from all of the books and all of the movies. On the other hand, honestly, you could make this [Sunrise] the first book you’ve ever read, or the first movie you’ve seen. You could start here, make it your jumping-off point, and then go in any order you wanted. So there’s accessibility for everyone.”

As for future stories, Lawrence and Jacobson are hopeful but note only Collins will know the answer.

“I don’t know if ‘superstitious’ is the right word, but she really does not let on whether or not she’s writing,” Lawrence says of Collins. “If she gets an idea and works on it, she keeps quiet, then turns it in to her publisher, who she trusts immensely, and waits to hear that it’s a publishable book. Only then does she tell us she’s written something.”

“I have not heard anything. Would I love her to write another book? Yes, I sure would, because I still love the world so much, and I still find there’s so much to learn,” Jacobson says. “Because she digs so deep in terms of both history and philosophy, I hope she still has so much more to say, and I hope she’ll decide to say it in Panem. But I don’t know. We haven’t gotten any winks or nods yet. I hope I get a wink and a nod, but I have gotten no winks, no nods so far.”

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is now in theaters.

#725. Germany gives sweeping powers to police, intelligence services

Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?

Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Germany's foreign intelligence service, will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.

Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Historian Sönke Neitzel of the University of Potsdam considers the separation principle understandable in its historical context. At the BKA's autumn conference, however, he described it as "nonsense" in light of today's threat landscape and said it was no longer necessary in a country that has been a constitutional democracy for decades.

While Neitzel considers the separation principle outdated, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU) wants to preserve it in its essential form. In his view, even a more extensive exchange of data does not violate the principle. At the same time, however, he has made clear that he wants to transform the domestically focused Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the BND into "real intelligence services."

This legislative reform brings Dobrindt a significant step closer to that goal. Parliament approved the interior minister's plans with the votes of the governing coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dobrindt insisted that Germany intends to take an active approach to defending itself against cyberattacks: "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back. They must know that their digital infrastructure, their server infrastructure, and their software will also be targeted by us."

BKA President Holger Münch welcomes Dobrindt's determination and points to the growing threat posed by cyberattacks. The line between criminal and state-sponsored actors is becoming increasingly blurred, he argues. As a result, both intelligence services and law enforcement agencies face the same challenge.

To underscore the scale of the threat as he sees it, Münch cited two statistics: in the first six months of 2026, crime originating from abroad rose by 24% compared with the same period the previous year. What concerns him most is that fewer than 5% of these cases are solved. The BKA chief considers this trend more dangerous than ever: "The state's promise of security can become fragile. Confidence in the ability of its institutions to act effectively and remain steadfast is declining."

This article was originally written in German.

#724. Creator Kennedy Eurich to Launch YouTube Series (Exclusive)

The digital series will debut in early 2027 on YouTube and across social media platforms.

Creator Kennedy Eurich is launching a new digital series on YouTube, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

The variety series, currently titled the Untitled Ken Eurich Project, is set to debut in early 2027 and will be distributed on YouTube and other social media platforms. The show will feature a mix of guests and hidden camera segments. The creator has secured independent financing to the tune of seven figures.

Eurich, known to followers as Ken, has nearly 2 million followers on TikTok alone, with much of her content focusing on speaking directly to the audience content. She has a secondary account with over 800K followers on TikTok, with another half a million followers on Instagram.

Like many creators working today, she’s been no stranger to brand deals. She’s partnered with brands like Cetaphil, Redken, Celsius, Coach and Tory Burch and partnered on ads with DoorDash, Popeyes and Torchy’s Tacos. She’s also hosted and done content for Tory Burch’s SS27 runway show and the 2025 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show.

The creator will allocate a portion of the show’s revenue to animal welfare initiatives through the Dallas-based Camillo Foundation, a private 501(c)(3) grantmaking foundation, according to a release.

Eurich is represented by CAA, OS Talent and Brecheen Feldman Breimer Silver and Thompson.

"This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its plan to place mirrors in Earth orbit to produce and sell sunlight after dark.

The goal is to extend the hours and output of solar farms globally, "making clean power dispatchable and available when you need it," the California-based startup explains on its website.

Reflect Orbital has made significant progress to date. On Tuesday (Nov. 10), for example, the company announced it had secured $73.5 million in new funding, boosting its total raise to more than $100 million. It has also gotten a formal go-ahead from the U.S. government to try out the concept in space and is currently readying its first test satellite, which is expected to launch in the second quarter of 2027. The identity of the launch provider is being kept under wraps at this time, the firm told Space.com.

Reflect Orbital recently conducted a ground-based test in California, lighting up a mountainous area to practice search and rescue (SAR) techniques.

On Oct. 10, the space startup set up spotlights near Lone Pine, California to simulate the illumination its proposed satellites could provide — controlled lighting without the need for any ground infrastructure. "This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power," the company explained in an Oct. 14 statement.

The October illumination test ran from 7 p.m. to midnight and involved members of the China Lake Mountain Rescue Group (CLMRG), who practiced with night-time equipment.

CLMRG is an all-volunteer activity, operating under the auspices of the Kern County Sheriff's Office providing SAR services on an on-call basis at no cost.

"Together with local search-and-rescue and disaster response groups, we carried out a fully permitted nighttime demonstration of our responsive lighting service," a Reflect Orbital spokesperson told Space.com in response to an inquiry about the exercise. "Search-and-rescue and disaster response teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who will use our technology."

Mobile lighting gear was mounted on Horseshoe Meadows Road to provide a spot of light similar to the ones that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. "The aim was to create a precise, realistic simulation of our service, so emergency responders could see how it will perform in real scenarios," Reflect Orbital said.

The brightness of the spot was roughly 0.7 lumens.

Reflect Orbital added that it will keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever the company operates, to show how its technology can help save lives.

"We're committed to learning incrementally about our technology and its impacts, and from potential customers and stakeholders, ahead of our planned satellite operations," the company stated.

In last month's illumination experiment, Reflect Orbital secured permits in advance, filed a NOTAM (a notice to pilots), notified Edwards Air Force Base and coordinated with the local sheriff's department. Area residents were also notified about the test ahead of time.

In a related development, Reflect Orbital has announced the purchase of two Skyroot Aerospace launches to deploy some of its spacecraft. Skyroot's Vikram-1 launcher is a product of India's private space sector, first flying from the nation's Sriharikota launch site last July. That flight was a landmark success, as Vikram-1 became the first private Indian rocket ever to reach orbit.

"These dedicated launches provide assured schedule and capacity, and complement Reflect Orbital's other planned launches from sites in the United States," Reflect Orbital explained in a different Oct. 14 statement.

Reflect Orbital says its approach is "incremental and test-and-learn." The company has been granted a license from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for one satellite. That mission will test the technology, including built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the sunlight service is delivered.

"It will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites," Reflect Orbital said, "the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions."

Reflect Orbital wants to be operating at least 50,000 of its mirror satellites in orbit by 2035. Not surprisingly, many people in the astronomy and stargazer communities have a dim view of this plan, saying it will generate light pollution that significantly degrades the night sky.

Reflect Orbital counters that most people and most places will never see this light. Customers will require permits, signoff from local authorities and "Know Your Customer compliance" to receive the service. Every service will require multi-layer approval, the company says, and if people do not want the light, they will not receive it.

Reflect Orbital also claims that it can maintain exclusion zones covering astronomical observation sites.

"Our satellites will be default-off when idle and constellation vehicles are designed to stay under +7 stellar magnitude for all non-serving attitudes. We're able to dim the brightness of the service and turn it off at any stage," the company's website states.

Reflect Orbital also notes that it's an industry member of the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Center for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky.

The company says that it's collaborating with the IAU on an observing campaign for when the service is operational and is also working on a coordination agreement with the U.S. National Science Foundation.

"We've engaged extensively with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other stakeholders," Reflect Orbital stated. "Their feedback has meaningfully informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans. We continue to welcome scientific exploration of how novel technology could deliver a lot of benefits to the world."

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. #721. Mathematician says he and AI solved Riemann hypothesis — the field’s biggest outstanding challenge

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Riemann hypothesis has been a lodestar for generations of mathetmaticians. Credit: James Brittain/Getty

In a year that has seen artificial intelligence reach one spectacular mathematical breakthrough after another, Anthropic is now claiming the top prize of them all: a full proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the statement that many mathematicians consider the most important open problem in the field.

The announcement came from Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the San Francisco, California company. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote, referring to Anthropic’s large language model (LLM).

“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford, UK, says.

It would also be a spectacular bicentenary present for Bernhard Riemann, the German mathematician who was born 200 years ago this September and who formulated the problem, which addresses the distribution of prime numbers, in the mid-1800.

The problem has to do with the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter zeta), which encodes the randomness properties of the prime numbers. Riemann discovered that the distribution of primes is encoded in the ζ function’s ‘zeroes.’ These are points on a plane denoted by z satisfying the equation ζ(z) = 0.

Riemann conjectured that apart from some obvious but uninteresting cases, all such solutions had to lie on a certain vertical line in the plane. If this were true, he showed, it would imply that prime numbers are scattered among all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as random as it could be.

Alpöge’s 4-page document includes a sketch of the proof. But Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada, says that Alpöge should have taken the time to prepare a clearer write-up before making the announcement, which came just days after Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO). The IPO initially valued the company at US$1.5 trillion, but the company’s valuation dropped on 19 November.

“What he released is garbled,” Granville says of Alpöge’s document. He cites the downturn in the company’s stock value as the reason for the timing of the proof’s release.

“There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false,” Alpöge wrote in the document.

Anthropic did not respond immediately to Nature’s request for comment.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03812-7

#720. Catholic Girls’ School Thriller ‘On Top of the Cliff’ Wins Top Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival Award

'When She Hears the Bells,' 'Pop Pop,' 'The Matriarch,' 'One Sweet Hour' and 'How to Divorce During the War' are also among the winners of the 30th anniversary edition of the Estonian festival.

Peruvian filmmaker Enrica Pérez’s Catholic girls’ school thriller On Top of the Cliff won the top award, the Grand Prix, in the main competition of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) and also earned Bianca Bucelli the best actress award for her performance in the movie.

In the atmospheric suspense drama, a worldly teen challenges a strict boarding school’s resident “holy” girl.

The best director honor went to Swiss writer-director Fred Baillif for his cinematic blend of fiction and documentary, A Job Well Done, which dives into the complexities and moral ambiguity that social workers working with immigrants face. Related Stories Movies 'Sh*t Happens' Is Full of Dark Humor, But Its Director Knows It Will Cause a Stink in the DR TV Netflix Renews Japanese Crime Hit 'Tokyo Swindlers' for Season 2

In the performance categories of the main competition, Bucelli was joined by Mathisse De Sutter, who won the best actor honor for his screen debut in Patrice Toye’s The Assignment. The jury lauded “the tenderness and emotional depth” he brought to the cinematic exploration of masculinity in the aftermath of war.

The jury, led by two-time Oscar-winning screenwriter and director Christopher Hampton (Dangerous Liaisons, Atonement), also featured Lebanese producer Myriam Sassine, U.S. cinematographer and visual effects specialist David Stump, French producer Julie Billy and Estonian actress Tiina Tauraite.

The jury lauded On Top of the Cliff for its strengths across the board. “Among a number of extremely accomplished entries, the jury was especially impressed by the high quality of every department of this film – direction, script, acting, cinematography, design and music – combining to create a hermetic universe, intense, powerful and visually eloquent,” it said.

In PÖFF’s First Feature Competition, Chabname Zariab’s When She Hears the Bells won the best film award. The film stars Golshifteh Farahani as a widow in Kabul, Afghanistan, who is fighting the exploitation of kids as the Taliban nears the city.

Young U.S. filmmaker Dylan Stephen Levers’ debut feature Pop Pop, which explores the manosphere and radicalization in the digital age, took the top prize in Tallinn’s Rebels With a Cause section.

Meanwhile, Maya Vitkova-Kosev’s One Month won the best film honor in PÖFF’s Critics’ Picks Competition. The coming-of-middle-age film tells the story of artist Sarah, 45, whose parents surprise her with a shocking ultimatum: After a lifetime of being protected and supported, she has one month to leave the family home.

And in the Baltic Film Competition, Andrius Blaževičius’ Lithuanian Oscar entry How to Divorce During the War won the best feature film award. The jury for the section highlighted the film’s ability to find humor amid difficult circumstances and “weave the personal and political into everyday details.” The honor makes Blaževičius the first two-time winner of the award after his 2021 win for his feature Runner.

Of course, the inaugural Free World Award, unveiled by PÖFF and the Odesa International Film Festival earlier this week to recognize “cinema that champions freedom, human dignity and human rights,” went to Halkawt Mustafa’s No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman. The award is made from melted weapons metal.

And the 2026 Audience Award went to Louis Paxton’s The Incomer.

Among the other honorees and special mention recipients on Friday night were also such features highlighted in THR‘s Tallinn coverage as The Matriarch, One Sweet Hour, Exotic, Arrow for A Stone Heart, Night Vision, Father’s House, and Princess.

Check out the full Tallinn 2026 winners list below.

#719. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.

It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.

At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.

It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.

"I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.

"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.

"I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever."

"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.

"The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.

"We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.

"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event."

"I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!"

"I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep."

"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away"

"I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.

"My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.

"He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.

"I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.

"That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.

"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.

"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting."

Not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.

Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas.

"Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'

"Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars."

Rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to New York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.

But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.

"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'"

The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.

Most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm.

The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The shows aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.

A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.

For now, we'll just have to wait and see.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.
