Astronauts get tasked with all kinds of weird science aboard the International Space Station. Recently, NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins got to work supporting an ongoing experiment that includes 3D-printing human cells and tissues in space.

Aboard the space station, astronauts have a multitude of responsibilities ranging from station maintenance and repairs on spacewalks to daily exercise and a wide variety of scientific research.

Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media.

In the image she is gloved-up with both her hands and arms covered in the sealed glovebox while she mixes samples of living cells with a bioink, a mixture she then inserts into a specialized cartridge, NASA shared.

This experiment that Watkins is working on "leverages the microgravity environment of ISS to 3D print cells and manufacture human liver, kidney, and cartilage tissue. Just one of many examples of how we’re using this amazing orbital national laboratory to reshape our understanding of biology, medicine, and engineering, and improve life on Earth!" Watkins shared online.

This experiment is designed to explore 3D printing human cartilage tissue in microgravity. The experiment aims to one day support future human patients both in space and on Earth.

When you think of the research that happens in space, 3D-printing human cells might not be the first thing to come to mind. But because of the unique microgravity environment onboard the ISS, it is the perfect home for even the strangest of biological experiments.

On the space station, there is still gravity but objects (and people) remain in a sort of constant freefall, leading to total weightlessness that mimics the complete absence of gravity. This weightlessness allows researchers to test, experiment and explore beyond the gravitational confines of Earth.

It’s a big week of honours at Billboard Canada as the 2026 40 Under 40 list has also dropped.

From independent label heads and managers building robust domestic infrastructure to scale talent globally, to live promoters championing community, the honourees are helping Canadian artists thrive at home and on the global stage.

From making beats in his bedroom to climbing the ranks of Montreal’s nightlife scene, he’s made history in the dance world with his forward-thinking, signature blend of R&B, funk and hip-hop. “Coming from Saint-Hubert [Quebec] and Montreal, then crossing over internationally, it’s not just anything,” he says in an interview with Billboard Canada. “I celebrate everything and I’m happy with still being a force in electronic music. I never take it for granted.”

Your mid-twenties are a period of major transformation — just ask Gracie Abrams.

“There’s this kind of lust and regret, and you see your own patterns as you evolve and enter new relationships or friendships,” the chart-topping singer-songwriter tells Billboard Canada from a New York hotel.

Those ideas are central to the artist’s second No. 1 album on the Billboard Canadian Albums chart, Daughter from Hell. Today (Nov. 20), she expands the universe with five deluxe tracks, deepening the album’s exploration of change and growth during the transformative decade

Extending the album’s lifecycle and building onto that world, she explains, has always cosmically aligned with her going on tour.

“That feels like the final form of the album to me, when we’re in community around it,” she says.

A memory that Abrams vividly remembers is when The Secret of Us and “That’s So True” went No. 1 back-to-back on the Nov. 23, 2024 and Nov. 30, 2024-dated Billboard Canada charts when she was an opening act on the final leg of Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour.

“I have such core memories about my Canadian audience because we’ve had some nuts milestones while we’ve been in Canada,” she says. “When [The Secret of Us] went No. 1, we got to be on stage and I got to say thank you to that many Canadian people [at sold-out Rogers Centre in Toronto]. I was so grateful that I could directly say it.”

She continues: “I just find it insane that people outside of your own village know who you are. It feels very lucky. The generosity and energy that we’ve been shown by our Canadian audience has blown my mind.”

Abrams pinpoints her two appearances at Montreal’s Osheaga, calling them “a core memory.” The sets bookmarked two different times in her career. She first performed in 2022 during the day on one of the main stages, and later was slotted for an evening set in 2025 on the same stage, but drew a much larger near-headline crowd.

#713. What's going on with the polar vortex?

Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

Voyager 1 has gone farther than any other object built by humanity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft.

The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth. And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).

NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.

To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code: NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence.

The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said.

NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making.

The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes.

Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2, is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.)

The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. On Thursday (Nov. 19) at 12 p.m. EST (1700 GMT), NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with Voyager mission team members and NASA leadership.

The discussion will cover the current status of both Voyager spacecraft, the unique scientific observations they continue to collect in interstellar space and the engineering challenges involved in keeping the nearly 50-year-old probes operational. A question-and-answer session with members of the media and audience will follow. NASA will also offer a preview of an upcoming Voyager documentary planned for release in 2027, coinciding with the mission's 50th anniversary.

For a mission that has carried humanity's message into interstellar space for nearly half a century, the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day” offers a chance for people back on Earth to mark just how far these pioneering spacecraft have traveled. More details about NASA's automated VGR flasher and step-by-step Morse code instructions are available online.

I am grateful for every moment of it, and I will always be cheering for Hello Sunshine.”

Neustadter has served as president of film and television at Hello Sunshine since she joined the company in 2017. Over her tenure, she executive produced a number of TV series, including The Morning Show, Big Little Lies, Little Fires Everywhere, The Last Thing He Told Me, Truth Be Told and Surface — also spearheading adaptations of Reese’s Book Club picks Tiny Beautiful Things and Daisy Jones & The Six. This past summer, Hello Sunshine premiered Legally Blonde prequel Elle at Prime Video and Lucky on Apple TV. Neustadter also worked on features Where the Crawdads Sing, Your Place or Mine, You’re Cordially Invited and TriStar’s upcoming adaptation of The Nightingale. She will remain with the company through the end of the year to support the transition.

Her departure comes during a period of transition for Hello Sunshine. In October, Witherspoon teamed up with Mediawan to buy the company back from Candle Media. Hello Sunshine, which Witherspoon founded with Seth Rodsky in 2016, was acquired by the Blackstone-backed company in 2021 in a deal valued at $900 million.

In partnering with the growing French media company, Hello Sunshine joins a sprawling portfolio of entertainment brands that includes Chernin Entertainment and Plan B Entertainment. But the shift has also meant changes at the company. Hello Sunshine’s sale was followed by layoffs its direct-to-consumer division.

Prior to her near-decade at Hello Sunshine, Neustadter worked at old Fox — where she was senior vice president of programming at the broadcast network, overseeing such series as The Mindy Project and Brooklyn Nine-Nine. She joined the network after a tenure at 20th Century Fox, where she worked on such films as Parental Guidance and Witherspoon vehicle This Means War. While at 20th, she was included The Hollywood Reporter’s Next Gen list — the magazine’s annual assessment of the 35 fastest rising entertainment executives under the age of 35.

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. The lives of NASA's Apollo astronauts depended on it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff.

First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

But a lunar liftoff? That was something new.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

"This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation."

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

#707. The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture

Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years and that he was looking at "broader" European security architecture before he was to fly to Abu Dhabi.

That sent off alarm bells in European capitals, with diplomats having pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine.

They feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

"There is no obvious compromise — dismantling NATO and the EU is not an option for Europe," said Maria Snegovaya, an expert on Russia at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.

"Repeatedly offering Putin peace deals he is unwilling to accept will not produce that outcome," Snegovaya said.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

#706. TV Ratings: CMA Awards Score Seven-Year High

The show delivers its biggest audience of the 2020s so far.

The 60th CMA Awards delivered their largest TV audience of the decade.

The Nov. 18 awards averaged 7.62 million viewers on ABC and Disney+, the best same-day total for the awards since 2019 (when it brought in more than 11 million viewers). Wednesday’s show finished just ahead of the 7.57 million viewers for the 2022 awards — with the caveat that Nielsen has made several changes to the way it measures ratings in the years since then.

The CMA Awards drew a 1.01 rating among adults 18-49 (equivalent to about 1.37 million people in the demographic), the first time the show has cleared a 1.0 rating since 2022. The telecast grew by 26 percent in viewers and 55 percent in adults 18-49 from a year ago (6.04 million viewers, 0.65 rating in the 18-49 demo). Related Stories TV Streaming Ratings: Rough Week for Original Series, 'From' Remains No. 1 Overall Music Taylor Swift Performs "Our Song" and "I Knew It, I Knew You" at the CMAs

Ella Langley set a record with six wins at the awards, including entertainer of the year. Her long-running No. 1 hit “Choosin’ Texas” won CMA Awards for song, single and music video of the year.

Along with Langley’s big night, the CMA Awards featured a performance by Taylor Swift — her first at the ceremony since 2013 — and a tribute to Dolly Parton that featured Vince Gill and host Lainey Wilson performing a duet of “I Will Always Love You.” Several other artists paid tribute to Parton during the show and on the red carpet beforehand.

ABC’s annual Countdown to the CMAs special on Tuesday also earned multi-year ratings highs. Hosted by Robin Roberts, the show drew just under 3 million viewers, its best showing since 2023.

"Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update.

The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.

The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)

That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.)

NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).

#704. NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record. Despite the striking increase, scientists from NASA and NOAA say Earth's protective ozone layer is continuing its gradual recovery and remains on track to heal later this century.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a large circulation of winds that influences atmospheric conditions over Antarctica. They also emphasized that international efforts to reduce harmful chemicals have prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone in the stratosphere because it serves as Earth's natural "sunscreen," protecting living organisms from dangerous solar radiation. Unlike this beneficial layer high in the atmosphere, ozone near Earth's surface is a pollutant frequently associated with human activities.

Antarctica's Ozone Hole Reaches Its Largest Size in a Decade

The ozone hole reached its maximum extent on September 18, spreading across 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). This was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

"The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing," said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA's ozone research team at the agency's Goddard Space Flight Center. "But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven't seen in a decade."

Although the hole expanded to an extraordinary size, the results also demonstrate the benefits of decades of international environmental protections. Without reductions in chemicals known to destroy ozone, the affected area could have been substantially greater.

"The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak," Newman said.

How a Powerful Polar Vortex Accelerates Ozone Loss

Ozone depletion begins with chemicals released through human activities, particularly compounds containing chlorine and bromine. Atmospheric circulation transports these substances into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them apart. The released chlorine and bromine atoms then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in Antarctic stratospheric clouds, leading to the destruction of ozone.

A major factor in this process is the stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal band of strong winds that circles Antarctica. This circulation traps extremely cold air over the region, allowing the formation of the special clouds that help trigger ozone destruction. When the vortex becomes unusually strong or expansive, conditions favorable for ozone loss can persist across a larger area.

In 2026, atmospheric disturbances that would normally weaken the vortex were unusually subdued. This allowed the circulation to remain powerful and helped create a broader region where ozone could be destroyed.

"The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September," said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. "That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur."

NASA and NOAA Measure the 2026 Ozone Hole

Despite its exceptional geographic size, the 2026 ozone hole did not experience the same extreme levels of ozone loss observed during record-breaking events 10 or 20 years earlier.

To measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers launched instruments attached to weather balloons from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected readings using the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical device designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations showed that ozone levels directly above the South Pole fell to their lowest reading of 2026 on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

The Dobson unit is the standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone above a particular location. To illustrate the scale, 100 Dobson units would produce a layer of ozone just 1 millimeter thick, approximately the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone in the atmospheric column were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest ozone concentration ever measured over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Satellites provide another essential source of information. Since 1979, spaceborne instruments have helped scientists observe changes in the ozone layer and track its condition over time. The 2026 measurements included data from NASA's Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a joint NASA and NOAA mission.

Why Earth's Ozone Layer Is Still Recovering

Scientists say the latest observations reinforce evidence that international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals are working. Much of that progress can be traced to the Montreal Protocol, a global agreement adopted in 1987 to phase out substances responsible for damaging the ozone layer.

Under the agreement, countries committed to replacing harmful compounds such as chlorofluorocarbons with alternatives that pose less danger to atmospheric ozone. According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting chemicals have declined by approximately one-third compared with their peak levels in the 1980s.

These reductions are significant because chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common in refrigerators, air conditioning systems, building insulation, and other everyday products. Although many of these substances have been phased out, they can remain in the atmosphere for decades. Additional emissions can also occur when older equipment, materials, and landfill waste release chemicals that were manufactured years ago.

Because these compounds break down so slowly, repairing the ozone layer takes many decades. Nevertheless, continued monitoring by NASA and NOAA indicates that the long-term recovery is progressing. Even with unusually large seasonal ozone holes such as the one observed in 2026, scientists expect the Antarctic ozone hole to recover by the 2070s.

The latest findings illustrate how exceptional atmospheric conditions can temporarily produce severe ozone depletion without reversing decades of environmental progress. They also highlight the lasting impact of international cooperation in protecting Earth's atmosphere.

#703. Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). A display reminds those attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, of their goal: limiting global warming to 1.5 ºC.Credit: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty

Net zero is no longer enough. Among countries at the COP31 climate summit under way in Antalya, Turkey, there’s a growing recognition that meeting climate targets will require the world to go ‘net negative’, which means removal of more carbon dioxide from the air than is added.

Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris Agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years. Reaching net-zero status would halt the rise in temperatures. But only achieving net-negative status can bring temperatures back below the 1.5 °C threshold this century.

Can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions

Can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions

That reality has made net negative and the enormous amount of CO2 removal that would be needed to achieve it a prominent idea at the summit. A coalition of eight countries called the Group of Negative Emitters (GONE) has been working to convince other nations to adopt net-negative targets and get serious about CO2 removal. The group announced that it will be co-chaired by Denmark and Ethiopia, which is hosting next year’s climate summit and could put net negative at the top of the agenda.

“We are in an era of overshoot, and we have to do a lot in terms of removing carbon dioxide,” Ethiopian ambassador Samuel Addis Alemayehu said at a GONE event on 18 November, touting the nation’s progress on reforestation.

Some climate campaigners worry that CO2 removal technologies won’t work and that focusing on them could distract countries from cutting emissions. Despite those concerns, the latest draft of the main statement from COP31 recognizes that CO2 removal has a role in addressing the overshoot, and welcomes efforts to “urgently and rapidly” scale up development of removal methods.

According to a United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report1 released ahead of the meeting, the world can expect about 1.8 °C of warming this century, even in the most optimistic emissions scenario.

Every fraction of a degree above 1.5 °C raises the risk of climate disasters such as wildfires and powerful hurricanes. “COP31 will be judged a failure if we don’t address the overshoot,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the UN and chair of the Association of Small Island States, at a press briefing held during the summit.

Many countries at the meeting have discussed slashing emissions to limit the size and duration of the coming overshoot. Turkey has pushed to implement a target of 35% of global energy demand being met with electricity by 2035, a proposal that has gained support from more than 75 countries at the conference and is also included in the draft statement.

But the UNEP report estimates that to recover from overshoot, at least 330 billion tonnes of CO2 would have to be pulled out of the atmosphere this century after the world reaches net zero. Removing that much CO2 would require a vast expansion of existing efforts. Today, about two billion tonnes of CO2 per year are removed by nature-based projects such as reforestation, which takes advantage of the carbon absorbed by growing trees. Scaling up carbon removal quickly enough to achieve net negative and storing carbon in a more durable form will require technological CO2 removal solutions as well.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03789-3

United Nations Environment Programme. Limiting Overshoot: Navigating Exceedance of 1.5°C and Pathways Towards Return (UNEP, 2026).

#702. Melania Trump Stresses Humanitarian Efforts at Chic Premiere for Two-Episode Series Documentary Follow-Up

At a tight-security screening at New York's Lincoln Center Thursday night, the first lady's longtime collaborators celebrated how the Brett Ratner-helmed show allows her to tell her own story.

In late January, Amazon‘s Brett Ratner-directed Melania documentary debuted at the Kennedy Center in Washington amid crowds of demonstrators in the wake of the fatal shootings by ICE agents of Alex Pretti and Renée Good in Minneapolis. The president had also sparked backlash for his efforts to overhaul the Kennedy Center, including adding his name to the exterior, which are still playing out in court.

Thursday night, Melania: The Series, a two-episode follow-up, though part of the initial $40 million project, consisting of bonus footage, debuted at New York’s Lincoln Center. Those involved with the film and series downplayed any significance of the change in venue, noting the president and first lady’s ties to New York. But if there were demonstrators, they weren’t seen or heard by those inside the tight-security screening at Alice Tully Hall, though whether that’s due to people moving on or the premiere location remains an open question. Related Stories Business Trump's $15 Billion Defamation Suit Against The New York Times Moves Forward TV CBS Inks New Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors

The screening came just two weeks after the 2026 midterm elections saw Democrats score historic, surprise victories in a referendum on the president that will result in a change in party control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Still, Trump’s longtime adviser Marc Beckman previously teased that the docuseries, now streaming on Amazon’s Prime Video, would be a “total different experience, completely new.”

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the Melania: The Series premiere, Beckman explained how the filmmaking team determined what would go in the documentary and what would be for the series.

“We decided that we would bifurcate and isolate certain stories that we thought were suitable for the series that weren’t necessarily appropriate for the film,” Beckman said. “The reason they’re suitable for the series is because it gives us more time to unpack more of her storyline, more about her family, more about her career, more about philanthropy and also what happens right after the inauguration when she takes on the role of being first lady of the United States again.”

Melania: The Series producer Fernando Sulichin, who took on the same role on the documentary, added that the film “was about going into the inauguration, and this one is first lady in action and what she’s about, more intimate — not the preparation of becoming the first lady but being the first lady.”

Beckman likened the approach to what Trump’s team did with her 2024 self-titled memoir Melania.

“With the trade edition of the book, we tell the story and we have certain photos in it, and then the collector’s edition, it’s a completely different experience so the fans could get both and enjoy them,” he said. “That’s the same thing here.”

Though it was initially expected that the docuseries would arrive on Amazon’s Prime Video when the documentary began streaming in March, Beckman said that was “just the media speculating,” and insisted the timing of the series’ release was in keeping with the licensing deal with Amazon he negotiated for the film and series.

“The timing for the contract is exactly what we’ve done,” he told THR on the black carpet Thursday night. “I negotiated the contract, so trust me, there’s no delay.”

While the documentary film, which was released in theaters in late January, followed Trump in the two weeks leading up to the start of her husband’s second term as president, the docuseries, in which Trump answers softball questions about her daily routine, interests and beliefs, first focuses on her role as a wife and mother, including her relationship with the president, followed by an episode centered around her and the president’s trips to North Carolina in the wake of Hurricane Helene and Los Angeles after the 2025 wildfires.

The film, coming in the wake of Trump’s best-selling memoir, was seen as part of a launch of a lifestyle brand. The doc and series’ $40 million Amazon purchase sparked backlash that the tech giant was trying to curry favor with the White House, criticism likely to continue with the project’s latest extension.

And while the Lincoln Center screening boasted Trump’s signature black-and-white color palette, complete with a black carpet and white tables and flowers, as well as tickets and popcorn boxes featuring the first lady’s face, Beckman steered questions about a possible lifestyle company back to Trump’s humanitarian efforts, specifically her work brokering a ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine and her Fostering the Future initiative to provide resources and educational opportunities for foster kids.

“I think right now what she’s really proud of is how she’s helping children and people throughout the world,” Beckman said. “What she’s doing in America is so much more important than a lifestyle brand.”

And before the docuseries premiered, Trump spoke, from a black-and-white podium bearing her name, about the Ukraine ceasefire, connecting it to her own personal ethos and the series’ focus, and episode titles, of “Family & Trust” and “Pride & Honor.”

“We live in a world that never stops moving, but life’s greatest moments belong to those who can stand still,” she began. “In calmness, we can see beauty. In peace, we can see humanity. My work is demanding, and sometimes the challenges I face seem impossible. Still, even in the most difficult circumstances, I find the drive to achieve the impossible. I rely on my own strength and character, with conviction, courage and reckless determination. I found a way forward where others would not.”

“For a brief moment, the world stood still for Oleshky. Eight hundred lives were saved. After so many years of fighting, the ceasefire brought a little bit of sunshine into lives which had been in the shadows of fear and war. The moment was very powerful for me because fighting and conflict have no value to the families on either side. Peace is rational,” she continued. “In the Oleshky ceasefire, we see the power of family, the restoration of trust and the courage of young children who do not back down in the face of war. Family, trust, pride, honor are the values we all hold in our hearts; they are also the foundation of the personal story I’m going to share with you tonight as part of Melania: The Series.”

As Trump teased that the series offered the opportunity to “experience [her] world through a new lens,” Trump’s current and former colleagues said they hoped the show, like the documentary, let Trump tell her own story.

President Trump’s first-term adviser Kellyanne Conway said conceptually that the documentary and series were “so amazing.”

“She’s obviously a very private person who has a very public life and in my view a very positive impact and that story does not get told,” Conway told THR. “And that’s OK, so let her tell her own story.”

Fashion designer Hervé Pierre, who created the first lady’s inaugural gowns for the president’s first and second ceremonies, added, “She’s not mysterious, but she’s not all over the media all the time and I think when she does something like she just did with [Russia and Ukraine], it’s not, like, fluff. It’s a very specific mission. So I think it’s important. I hope we will discover something that we don’t know about her. And I think sometimes it’s better for her to [express something in her own words] than to have an interpretation of what she’s doing. At least you have a direct line.”

And what sort of things might viewers discover about Trump that they don’t already know?

Pierre, who’s long worked with the first lady, offered a couple of insights.

“She cries when she laughs,” he said of her tendency to tear up at humorous moments. “She’s very happy. I’ve worked with difficult women for 30 years in haute couture. She never, ever raised her voice or [had attitude]. She’s always in a good mood — it’s fascinating.”

#701. Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water

Earth may have created a substantial amount of its own water as the planet was forming, rather than relying entirely on comets, meteorites, or other objects to deliver it from space. New research published in Nature Geoscience suggests that chemical reactions between rocky pebbles and the hydrogen-rich atmosphere of the young Earth could have produced enormous quantities of water.

The discovery offers a new explanation for how our planet acquired one of the most important ingredients for life. It also raises the possibility that other rocky planets throughout the universe could generate water through similar processes, potentially making habitable worlds more common than previously thought.

Researchers at The University of New Mexico investigated this possibility by recreating some of the extreme conditions that existed during Earth's formation. The study was led by graduate student Susmita Garai, along with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson. Their experiments examined what happens when rocks containing iron react with hydrogen at extremely high temperatures.

"Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism," explained Sharp. "In order to evaluate the possibility of 'pebble' rain' being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai's efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the Early Earth's atmosphere."

A New Explanation for the Origin of Earth's Water

For decades, scientists have debated where Earth's water originally came from. One prominent theory suggests that much of it was transported to the developing planet by icy material originating in the colder, more distant regions of the early solar system.

According to this explanation, water-rich objects, including small icy pebbles, traveled inward and eventually contributed to Earth's water supply. However, researchers have struggled to fully explain how enough of this material could have reached our planet from such great distances. There are also unresolved questions about whether this delivery process accounts for Earth's chemical composition.

The new study investigates a different route by which water could have appeared. Instead of arriving already contained in ice or other materials, water may have been produced directly through reactions involving the rocky ingredients that built Earth and the gases surrounding it.

During the planet's earliest stages, countless small pieces of rock gradually came together to form a larger body. Scientists refer to this growth process as pebble accretion. As Earth gained mass, it could have accumulated a dense atmosphere containing large amounts of hydrogen, with temperatures and pressures far higher than those found on the planet today.

Under those conditions, rocky pebbles falling through the atmosphere could have triggered a remarkable chemical reaction. Hydrogen in the surrounding gas would react with iron oxide inside the silicate rocks, transforming the iron oxide into metallic iron while releasing water vapor.

Experiments Reveal Water Can Form in Minutes

To determine whether this process could actually occur, the researchers exposed samples of silicate rock to temperatures ranging from 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius. They conducted experiments using flowing hydrogen gas and repeated the tests with helium to provide a comparison. Each experiment ran for between 15 minutes and three hours.

The results provided strong evidence that the proposed reaction works under these extreme conditions. When the rocks were heated in hydrogen, almost 80% of their iron oxide was transformed into metallic iron, with water vapor produced during the reaction.

In contrast, the researchers did not observe the same reaction when helium was used instead of hydrogen. This difference confirmed that hydrogen played a crucial role in generating the water.

The speed and scale of the reaction were especially striking. Although the scientists had expected some water to form, the results suggested that the process could have been far more productive than anticipated. When they extended their experimental findings to conditions on the early Earth, their calculations indicated that the mechanism might have generated hundreds of oceans' worth of water.

"We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans' worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have," said Sharp.

Earth's Fiery Beginnings May Have Helped Create Its Oceans

These findings suggest that the conditions of Earth's formation may have actively contributed to its water supply. Rather than being entirely dependent on water delivered from elsewhere in the solar system, the growing planet may have possessed the ingredients needed to manufacture water through its own chemical reactions.

The implications extend well beyond Earth. If rocky planets around other stars develop similarly hot, hydrogen-rich atmospheres during their formation, they might also produce substantial amounts of water as rocky material accumulates.

This possibility could have important consequences for understanding how common water is across the universe. A process that naturally occurs during the formation of Earth-sized planets would mean that obtaining water might not require the right icy objects to arrive from distant regions of a planetary system.

Could Other Earth-Like Planets Make Their Own Water?

The research also adds to growing interest in pebble accretion as an explanation for how planets form. Although the concept has gained attention relatively recently, it has already helped scientists address several longstanding questions about planetary development.

"The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It's only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation," Sharp said. "And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life."

There are still important uncertainties to resolve. While the experiments show that rocky material can generate water when exposed to hydrogen under conditions resembling those of the early Earth, they do not establish how much of our planet's present water supply was actually produced this way. Additional research will be needed to determine the contribution of this mechanism compared with water delivered by comets, meteorites, and other sources.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important process that may have shaped Earth billions of years ago. They also suggest that the ability to produce water could be built into the formation of rocky planets themselves, opening new possibilities for understanding where water, and perhaps life, might exist beyond our solar system.

Materials provided by University of New Mexico. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.

Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.

However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.

The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.

"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.

Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.

This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #699. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the data.

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

This article was originally published in German.
