#698. ‘Yellowjackets’ Creators on Closing Their Survival Story, Killing Characters and Thoughts on Spinoffs: “This Was Meant to Be the Final End”

Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson hope to leave viewers satisfied when the fourth and final season of the Showtime hit releases its series finale: "We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that's important."

[This story contains mild spoilers from the premiere of Yellowjackets season four.]

The end is near for Yellowjackets. The fourth and final season of Showtime‘s hit survival story has begun, and the weekly drop of final episodes will send viewers on a wild ride as they ruminate on life, death — and the meanings behind those bizarre post-Yellowjackets dreams. If it’s any consolation, the creators have those dreams, too.

“Life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width,” Bart Nickerson, chatting with his co-creator wife, Ashley Lyle, tells The Hollywood Reporter of the last near-decade making the hit Showtime series. The pair initially planned for five seasons, but when the Paramount renewed Yellowjackets for a fourth and final season, the creators pivoted. Related Stories NEXT BIG THING Jasmin Savoy Brown Bids Farewell to 'Yellowjackets' and Finds Her Way to 'Hadestown' Lifestyle The Paramount+ Black Friday Deal Gets You Two Months for Less Than a Latte

“For us,” says Lyle, “it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. We took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably would have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.”

What they deliver is what viewers have been waiting for when the survivors of the Yellowjackets plane crash that began the series are rescued and returned home in the season four premiere. Following the teens as they reassimilate into life in New Jersey — while learning how to live with the murders and cannibalistic acts they harbor; the things they did to survive those months in the wilderness — delivers a fascinating watch and full-circle return to where this story began.

Below, Lyle and Nickerson dive into making the final season and what to expect, including the pain of killing off characters while always knowing who would survive in the end. They also explain why they aren’t interested in spinoffs — because they’re ending the story with a period, not an ellipses: “We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s important. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story.”

We have been waiting for this rescue season. When we spoke with you two way back in the beginning of all of this, in your heads, you had envisioned Yellowjackets as a five-season show, and here you are ending with four seasons.

How big of a pivot was this to wrap up the show earlier than you planned?

LYLE Ultimately, as we were breaking this season, we realized that it was workable. It came down to: Do we potentially overstay our welcome? Of course, when you’re making television, there’s always a risk that you will not get another season. So we realized at a certain point that there was a much more high-octane version of this season that could accomplish all the things that we really hoped to accomplish when we first conceived of the show.

Coming off of the third season, we always knew we wanted to get the girls back home. Then we always knew in the adult timeline that we wanted things to start turning in on itself amongst these women in their relationships. And it did feel like we had hit that pivot point at the end of season three. So we just ended up going full steam ahead; burden the hand. The ability to tell a complete story, to finish it on our own terms, is something we’re incredibly grateful for. We hope everyone feels a sense of satisfaction with this final season.

Given the narrative of viewers dropping off after two seasons of a show, did you feel like season three was the hardest point to keep your audience, and did that affect what you wanted to do going into four?

BART NICKERSON To be honest, I didn’t know that was a thing — that audiences drop after two season. I think, in some respect, through the entire run of the show, there is, as it turns out, a gift in being, tremendously insecure and scared. (Laughs.) Every script we’ve ever written, even if we’re just going to our writers group, you have so much of your personal self-worth and the quality of that script, you kind of live and die on every piece of feedback. Although it sounds insane, the stakes of making a season of television are almost a little intellectual — you don’t ever stand in front of the audience and hear them reacting to your thing. Because the stakes are always so high, it wasn’t about: How do we keep this going? Or: People didn’t like this, how do we address that? At the end of the day, you just have to make the story you’re trying to make for better or for worse. And some may say for worse! (Laughs.)

LYLE I don’t really understand the metrics of how they’re counting viewership at this point. I’m not sure anybody does. I think they said season three was the most watched, but some of that, I’m sure, is people catching up on Netflix. For us, it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. And we took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably would have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.

As the storytellers, you have a huge ensemble. So many stories to tell. What were some of the biggest challenges knowing that this was it? That you had a finite number of episodes left.

NICKERSON Yes, just that in and of itself [is the challenge]. We love television. We love telling television stories, and we love our characters and want them all to have a full, complete arc. Then there is the reality only having so many pages and so many minutes on screen. So it’s about how to be as efficient as possible, and that has always been a challenge. We’ve always wanted each episode, each season, each scene to have a beginning, middle and an end. So it’s about, how do you tell these stories with efficiency but also arc? That has always been an incredible challenge.

Did it leave more things on the cutting room floor? Anything you can share now that didn’t work or make the show?

LYLE Not necessarily in a macro sense for this season. Every episode, we’re always over time. We’ll sit with the editors and pull out 10 seconds at a time to get it under 60 minutes. You’re always cutting. That was the case in season one. That was the case in season two. Sometimes you go back and go, “Remember when that scene existed?” And the fact is that it was sort of telling you that it didn’t need to be there. So I think the process kind of works itself out as you go.

LYLE That’s a question for Paramount Skydance!

NICKERSON Having one less season [I don’t think changes that], because we came to an end that was meant to be the final end. There are always ideas you haven’t had yet. So, never say never. But there isn’t something where it’s like, because we had one last season, we could come back and revisit that.

Do you two feel like you are closing the Yellowjackets book with this ending? No ideas for a tangent or a right turn in any way?

LYLE We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s important. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story. I suppose in this day and age, there’s a never-say-never quality to this question, but at the same time, we wanted to tell a complete story. We wanted it to feel like the audience had been on the full ride. And hopefully, that there’s a lot of emotional satisfaction in the resolution that we find.

NICKERSON At the end of the day, there’s a level on which, if you’re telling a story about survival, you’re telling a story about death, and that means there has to be an end, because that’s what you’re confronting — the end-end. And, what does it mean when it’s over? I don’t think it would be possible to tell a satisfying ending if it didn’t feel like the ending … of everything … ever. (Laughs.)

You come out swinging with the season four premiere jumping right into the rescue timeline. You could have built your way up to it. Can you talk about why you wanted to lead with it, and fill in the gaps from the past as the season goes?

LYLE That is a storytelling paradigm we’ve always been drawn to: not necessarily the “what happens” but the “why.” That was a big part of season one with the question of whether or not they engage in cannibalism. There were people who said, did you ever consider teasing that out? And we’re like, “No.” We wanted to put it in the pilot, because to us, the most interesting thing wasn’t whether or not they’d do it. It was, why did they do it? How did they get there? What is the context for it?

Similarly, with this season, it was a clearing of the decks, a reset in a way that could set up this season as a standalone season. And again, it wasn’t if they get rescued, it’s how and why, and what happens in the aftermath?

We would talk in the writers room, now that we’ve got four timelines or (let’s just make things a little more complicated for ourselves!), in terms of post-rescue, pre-rescue and present day. And it felt like what happened in the interim between Natalie’s distress call and them getting rescued could serve much more effectively as a little bit of mystery. Because to us, the more important emotional heartbeat of this season was going to be the post-rescue: how they were coping with and the different ways they would personally strategize how they would handle the reintegration. That was a much more interesting question for us at this point.

So much has happened to these characters over the course of the series, but it’s also been almost a decade since you two started developing this show. Do you feel like you also have grown with the show, in terms of how you wanted to end it and what you want to say in the end?

NICKERSON Speaking for myself, yes, tremendously. It would be difficult for me to fully articulate what I mean, but so much of this story is a result of stuff that’s been churned up and has continued to churned up. I always say the best compliment that people will give us about the show is, “I just started watching Yellowjackets. My dreams have been so messed up!” This idea that there is a deepness to the show.

I’ve had some bizarre dreams while watching these screeners!

NICKERSON (Laughs.) That’s been our life for nine years! Just weird dreams. (Laughs.) I feel like life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width.

This show is about surviving and about death. There have been so many big deaths along the way. We still feel Juliette Lewis’ exit and last season, you took so many of them away! Fans are always reacting. How much did you take the fans into account when you thought about who is going to survive this season?

LYLE We didn’t. I don’t think we can, because, ultimately, if we were trying to please some segment of the audience, we’re going to displease another. We have to write it for ourselves and use that as a guiding light and principle. It’s a fool’s errand to try to do fan service, especially when you’re planning how to end a show.

NICKERSON The first time we met with Julie Plec, who gave us our first job in television, it was a couple days after a big character death in Vampire Diaries. It was like, “Oh, my God. I can’t believe you killed this person!” She got very serious and was like, “It’s my job to service the story before I service what the fans think they want.”

Because, ultimately, when I’m rooting for a character, I have this relationship with them. I’m not really thinking about the story. I’m thinking about the character and my relationship to them. In order to give the fans something of value, you have to keep your eye on what you’re trying to build and not necessarily on how it’s going to be received.

Your characters are like your babies. Is there a death that still sits with you or any character you wish you still had around to play with?

LYLE I think that speaks to what Bart was saying. They’re all difficult. But one that always comes back around as being rough for everybody involved on set was when we killed Coach Scott last season. Steven [Krueger] knew very early on — we go way, way, way back. He was like, “It’s time. I’m surprised I lasted this long.” There are moments where, man, you miss the character, you miss having that actor on set. But at the same time, it had to happen.

NICKERSON And that’s one of the moments I am most proud of. Every time we watched, it was such an incredible performance by both of them [Krueger and Sophie Thatcher]. It was amazing. The whole thing to watch the Natalie character born in this ultimate sacrifice that she’s making for somebody else, but it’s also a grisly, violent act. I so miss that character. But, what are we doing if it’s not trying to create those moments?

I know those calls to your departing actors have been difficult along the way, but I imagine dying in the final season is different. You probably get some cheering. It’s like a badge of honor.

Did you always know who would be the final girl(s), or did it change along the way?

NICKERSON My only hesitation is that, on the path, you investigate different things. But, no, it was at the beginning. At the beginning, this was how we were going to do it.

LYLE We kicked the tires a lot. But we really ended up in the place we thought we would.

NICKERSON Yeah. Some of the particulars changed. Ultimately, the meaning of it has, for me at least, shifted. But yeah, we actually did end up where we thought we would.

I know you can’t talk spoilers. But is there anything you want to tease… will dead characters return? Will we ever see that lost episode? Any surprises in store?

NICKERSON We’re not allowed to say! We want to reveal everything. We just want you to see it!

You have always talked about having big beats you knew you wanted to hit throughout the show: Pit Girl, the scientists, rescue. Anything you can’t wait for us to see, in broad terms?

NICKERSON I don’t think it’s a spoiler to say that them coming back to New Jersey has always been a huge thing we wanted to do, and, in some sense, is the show.

LYLE There are a few things. There’s a scene in episode five that we’ve been talking about for many seasons.

NICKERSON Oh yeah, that is going to be really good! We’ve been talking about for a really long time.

There have been more than one scene that made your actors unwell — and even had them throwing up. For example, the Jackie feast … the Pit Girl reveal. Was there any filming experience in this final season that’s comparable to that?

LYLE I think they toughened up a little bit.

NICKERSON I mean, eating Jackie was rough. That was a tough day!

LYLE That was really, really rough. I don’t know that we could ever top that, in terms of torturing our actors.

NICKERSON Because that thing [Jackie’s edible body] looked good. I mean, not tasty, but, oh man. Just to have what they were going to eat like around is tough.

LYLE There was a moment on set this season when Melanie [Lynskey] brought her daughter to set and sort of regretted it immediately. Like, “Oh, just kidding! Go into the trailer.” I was like, “That’s not real. It’s okay!” She seemed fine. I mean, we don’t have to pay for her therapy! (Laughs.)

Yellowjackets is now streaming the first episode of season four on Paramount+ Premium.

#697. AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City."

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!"

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

Molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

Molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel."

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

It’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard announced last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”

#695. A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret. For more than two centuries, scientists believed that the genus Colobura contained just one widespread species. Now, researchers have identified a third species that looks almost identical to its relatives, raising new questions about how these butterflies evolved and continue to live alongside one another.

The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History. By combining DNA analysis with subtle differences in wing patterns and ultraviolet light reflection, the team uncovered distinctions that had remained largely invisible to scientists.

Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time. Yet genetic evidence suggests they remain separate, with no detectable signs of interbreeding.

A Familiar Butterfly With a Hidden Identity

Central and South America's tropical rainforests contain some of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet. Costa Rica alone supports approximately half a million species, roughly five times the number found across Canada, even though Canada's land area is about 200 times larger.

Despite this extraordinary diversity, certain plants and animals are especially recognizable throughout the region. In Canada's boreal forests, balsam firs are a familiar feature of the landscape. In tropical America, trees belonging to the genus Cecropia play a similarly prominent role.

In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper described their importance, writing, "Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember Cecropia, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries."

The butterflies of the genus Colobura are just as recognizable, according to Sapkota.

"If you go to the neotropics, Colobura is one of the first butterflies you see," she said.

These butterflies and Cecropia trees share a close ecological relationship because Cecropia leaves provide food for Colobura caterpillars. Both groups occur across an enormous geographic area, from portions of the Andes Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon to the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay. They are also widespread throughout Central America and the Caribbean Islands.

Such broad distributions are not particularly unusual in tropical ecosystems. However, the diversity within these groups presents an interesting contrast.

Scientists recognize 61 species of Cecropia, many of which occupy relatively small geographic areas. Some grow only in the Andes, while others are confined to the Caribbean.

For Colobura butterflies, the situation appeared very different. After Carl Linnaeus formally described Colobura dirce in 1758, scientists spent more than 200 years treating the genus as a single species, despite its extensive range.

That understanding began to change in 2001, when researchers formally recognized a second species. Now, an unexpected discovery in Venezuela has led to the identification of a third, described by Sapkota and her colleagues in Zootaxa.

Rather than providing a simple explanation for the group's evolutionary history, the discovery has introduced an even greater puzzle.

"It's crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time."

A Butterfly Mystery Dating Back More Than 150 Years

Distinguishing adult Colobura butterflies is exceptionally difficult. Their wings are nearly identical, with only slight variations in a gray stripe on the underside of the front wings. In some butterflies, this stripe becomes a little wider. In others, it stays the same width. It may also extend far enough to meet a yellow band running across the wing, or stop short of it.

Their caterpillars offer somewhat clearer clues.

Colobura caterpillars have velvety black bodies covered with prominent yellow projections that end in sharply angled barbs. These defensive structures send a warning to potential predators that could be interpreted as "leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences."

Beneath those conspicuous spines are much smaller cream-colored markings. Depending on the species, these markings may resemble teardrops or rings, or they may be missing entirely.

The importance of these differences was recognized surprisingly early.

In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp proposed that caterpillars with different cream-colored patterns represented two separate species. Other researchers rejected his interpretation, arguing that the variations could reflect differences between males and females or simply natural variation within a single species.

That view remained dominant for approximately 150 years.

In 2001, Keith Willmott and several colleagues revisited Sepp's observations and formally described a second species, Colobura annulata. Willmott is now a curator at the Florida Museum's McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity.

"We assumed that was the problem solved," Willmott said.

He moved on to other research, believing the longstanding classification problem had been resolved. However, occasional observations continued to suggest that something was missing.

"I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible."

At the time, even the existence of two nearly indistinguishable species seemed remarkable.

"It's a very distinctive butterfly. It's hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they're so different from anything else."

Roughly 25 years later, fresh evidence emerged when Willmott's colleague Andrés Orellana encountered a group of hungry Colobura caterpillars feeding on a young Cecropia tree in Venezuela.

The caterpillars were rapidly stripping leaves from the sapling. They possessed the familiar black body segments near the head and yellow spines characteristic of the genus, but one feature stood out.

Unlike the two recognized species, these caterpillars had no cream-colored markings at all.

Orellana photographed the unusual insects and shared the images with Willmott. The discovery provided a compelling reason to investigate whether a third species had been overlooked.

Sapkota had recently joined the Shirey lab at the Florida Museum and was eager to lead the investigation.

Working with her colleagues, she designed a study that combined genetic evidence with careful examinations of butterfly anatomy.

First, she studied DNA barcodes, short and highly variable genetic sequences that help researchers distinguish species. These sequences came from a long-running survey of butterflies and moths in Costa Rica led by study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs.

The investigation then expanded to older butterfly specimens collected across tropical Central and South America. Sapkota sent these museum samples to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, where researchers sequenced both their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

The genetic results provided a way to test whether the butterflies represented genuinely different evolutionary groups rather than ordinary variations within a single species.

But the researchers also wanted to know whether there were physical differences that previous scientists had failed to notice.

An Invisible Clue Hidden in Butterfly Wings

Sapkota spent hours examining preserved butterflies in museum collections, searching for consistent traits that might distinguish the suspected species.

At first, the effort produced few answers. Other than the slight differences in the gray wing stripe, the butterflies appeared remarkably similar.

Eventually, she noticed something unusual.

The undersides of some wings appeared to have a faint violet shimmer, and the intensity of that sheen seemed to vary between specimens.

This observation suggested that the insects might reflect ultraviolet light, which falls outside the range of human vision but can be detected by many butterflies.

"I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn't look violet to me, it reflected UV light," she said.

The measurements revealed a striking pattern. All three species reflected ultraviolet light, but the wavelengths differed.

The researchers named the newly identified species Colobura cryptica, reflecting its previously concealed identity.

Although the visible differences were extremely subtle, the ultraviolet measurements, caterpillar markings, and DNA results told a consistent story.

The three species could be distinguished by the following features:

There is an additional complication with Colobura dirce. It includes two subspecies with different ultraviolet reflectance values. Colobura dirce dirce reflects light at 362.2 nm, while Colobura dirce wolcotti reflects light at 390.6 nm. The 376 nm value represents the average for the species.

Beyond these minor wing differences, Sapkota could not identify any other consistent anatomical distinctions. Even the male genitalia, which often provide some of the most reliable features for separating butterfly and moth species, appeared indistinguishable.

Nevertheless, the genetic findings were decisive.

DNA analysis identified three distinct evolutionary lineages, and those divisions matched the physical differences the team had documented. Together, the evidence confirmed that Colobura contains three species rather than two.

Three Butterfly Species Living Side by Side

Identifying a previously unknown butterfly species is significant on its own, but the geographic distributions of these three species make the finding particularly intriguing.

All three occur in overlapping portions of Central and South America.

Colobura dirce has the widest distribution, extending from Mexico to southeastern Brazil. It occurs on both sides of the Andes Mountains and throughout the Caribbean archipelago.

Colobura annulata also occupies a large geographic area, although it is absent from the Greater Antilles.

The newly described Colobura cryptica has the smallest known range, stretching from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.

These overlapping distributions raise an important evolutionary question. How did three species become genetically distinct while continuing to occupy many of the same regions?

Species often emerge when populations become isolated from one another. A mountain range, for example, might divide a population and prevent individuals on opposite sides from mating.

Over many generations, the separated groups can accumulate different genetic and physical traits. If those differences become great enough, the populations may eventually lose the ability to interbreed, even if they come into contact again.

But geographic separation is not the only mechanism that can drive the formation of new species.

Researchers suspect that the Colobura butterflies might have developed different ways of using their shared forest habitats.

"There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies," Sapkota said. "Colobura dirce is typically found in the undergrowth and C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies."

In other words, one species may spend more time near the forest floor while the others favor the upper branches.

This kind of habitat separation could potentially help maintain differences between species living in the same geographic area.

However, previous research has produced inconsistent observations. One reason may be that even experienced butterfly specialists have difficulty telling the three species apart.

How Do Nearly Identical Butterflies Recognize Each Other?

An even more puzzling question concerns how the butterflies identify suitable mates.

Many moths and some butterflies use special scent glands to release pheromones, chemical signals that help individuals recognize members of their own species.

That suggests visual information may play an important role in mate selection. Yet their nearly identical appearance makes it difficult to understand how they distinguish one species from another.

The newly discovered ultraviolet differences offer a possible explanation.

Although humans cannot see ultraviolet light, many butterflies can. Sapkota suspects that the different ultraviolet reflections from their wings might provide visual signals that help them identify members of their own species.

Similar mechanisms are known or suspected in other butterflies and moths. Garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths possess ultraviolet-reflecting wing scales that researchers believe may contribute to mate selection.

Sapkota is investigating whether Colobura butterflies use comparable signals, but the results have not yet provided a clear answer.

Whatever mechanism they use, the butterflies appear remarkably successful at maintaining their separate identities.

Analysis of nuclear DNA found no evidence of hybridization among the three species, despite their overlapping ranges.

The findings suggest that the species have followed separate evolutionary paths without detectable genetic mixing.

A Familiar Butterfly Still Holds Many Secrets

The discovery of Colobura cryptica demonstrates how much remains unknown about even widespread, conspicuous animals.

For generations, naturalists studied these butterflies without recognizing the full diversity hidden within the group. Only by combining detailed observations with modern genetic testing and ultraviolet measurements were researchers able to uncover the third species.

Yet some of the most important questions remain unanswered, including how the butterflies choose mates, whether they occupy different parts of the forest, and what originally caused their evolutionary separation.

For Sapkota, answering those questions will require observing the insects in their natural habitats.

"Someone has to go the field to find it out themselves."

Those interested in another unusual aspect of Colobura biology can explore the Biodiversity Heritage Library, which contains a whimsical account published in 1952 describing the poop perches that young Colobura caterpillars construct during their earliest developmental stages.

Additional study co-authors include Andrés Orellana of the Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira; Nick Grishin and Leina Song of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Isidro Chacón of the Museo Nacional Santo Domingo de Heredia; Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs of the University of Pennsylvania; and Sajan KC of the Florida Museum of Natural History.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Welch Foundation, Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (NFRFt-2020- 00073), the Canada Foundation for Innovation's Major Science Infrastructure program (MSI 42450), BioAlfa, and Project UNET (Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira).

#694. Marvel’s ‘Blade’ Director Exited Failed Movie Because ‘Life’s Too Short to Make S— Films’ and It Was ‘Dangerous’ Working ‘Without a Proper Script’

Bassam Tariq revealed in a new interview with The New Arab that the biggest lesson he learned as the original director of Marvel’s failed “Blade” movie is “life’s too short to make shit films.”

“It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script,” Tariq said abot his short-lived Marvel career. “You’re sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you. That’s also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn’t add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot. All I have is my integrity, and I’ve been thinking about that a lot.” Related Stories Priyanka Chopra Jonas, Russell Crowe Sci-Fi Thriller 'Bluefly' Adds 'Beast' Star Daniel MacPherson (EXCLUSIVE) 'Beast in Me' Season 2 Casts Riley Keough, Lorelei Olivia Mote, Aaron Paul, Taip Ceman, Matthew James Thomas

“If you’re the bearer of bad news to your actors, but you’re not the one making any of these decisions — and it’s actually coming from a corporate entity — that’s not a great way to be a director,” the director continued. “I know some people can take that and run with it, but I learned I was losing credibility with my actors, and it wasn’t a healthy way to operate as a filmmaker. Life’s too short to make shit films, so that was my big lesson: I have to have full control over my script. If we disagree, it’s between them and me. It’s quite sad because we had such high hopes for what we wanted to build.”

Marvel originally announced “Blade” at Comic-Con in July 2019 with Oscar winner Mahershala Ali set to star in the title role. Tariq (who went on to direct Ali in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”) was the first director to join the movie, but he exited in September 2022 roughly two months before it was set to begin shooting. Yann Demange stepped in as the movie’s director after Tariq’s exit, but Demange ended up dropping out in June 2024.

Variety reported in November 2023 that “Blade” had gone through at least five different writers while in development, from “Watchmen” scribe Stacy Osei-Kuffour to Michael Starrbury. The movie was ultimately scrapped and never went into production.

Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige told the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast over the summer that he was “feeling like a gigantic loser and failure” for failing to get Ali’s “Blade” made, to which Ali agreed with during a later interview with GQ magazine.

“That’s a Kevin Feige question,” Ali said when asked why Marvel never got to the point of putting “Blade” into production. “They had, as you said, a two-time Oscar-winning actor under contract and you got billions of dollars. That’s a question for them. I don’t mean anything personal to you, but I don’t know why it didn’t. To this day, I don’t know why it didn’t happen. I just know that it was—Kevin, he said it was the biggest failure of his career and I agree.”

Amid the film’s development struggles, Ali’s interest in playing Blade never wavered. He told Variety on the “Jurassic World Rebirth” red carpet in 2015: “I’m ready. Let them know I’m ready.” In an interview with GQ earlier this year, Ali called out Marvel point blank by saying: “You had me under contract, they have billions of dollars, if they wanted to do the movie, we would’ve done the movie. So we’re not doing the movie.”

Feige explained in July 2025 how the prolonged delays on “Blade” were a symptom of Marvel’s “over-expansion” into Disney+ streaming content where “for the very first time ever, quantity trumped quality.” When Marvel began to reevaluate its development process, the “Blade” movie was one of the projects that stalled.
